orig_quadratics_factorisation.description: Solve quadratic equations by factorisation, the quadratic formula and substitution. Work through examples and check every valid root in 9709 Pure 1 practice.

sections.title: What makes an equation quadratic?
sections.label: Recognise a quadratic equation
sections.intro: Find every real value of \(x\) that makes the original equation true.

blocks.html: A quadratic equation can be written as \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\), where \(a\ne0\). The numbers \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are the coefficients, including their signs.

Factorise and solve mean different things

To factorise an expression, rewrite it as a product:

\[x^{2}-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3).\]

To solve an equation, find the values of the variable:

\[\begin{gathered}x^2-5x+6=0\\ x=2\text{ or }x=3.\end{gathered}\]

The first statement is true for every value of \(x\). The second equation is true only for its roots.

retry.feedback: Move the linear term to the left. Its sign changes.

blocks.html:
Which method should I choose?

  • Factorise when a common factor or suitable brackets are easy to find.
  • Use the formula when factorisation is inconvenient.
  • Complete the square when a square form is useful or the question requests it.
  • Substitute when the equation is quadratic in another expression, such as \(x^{2}\) or \(\sqrt{x}\).

Before changing an equation, note any restrictions: a denominator cannot be zero, and a real square root needs a non-negative number inside it.

sections.title: How do I solve a quadratic by factorising?
sections.label: Factorise and find the roots
sections.intro: Make one side zero, write the other side as a product, then solve each factor.

blocks.html:
Set each factor containing \(x\) equal to zero.

\[AB=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A=0\ \text{or}\ B=0.\]

First make one side zero. From \((x-2)(x-3)=6\), the zero-product rule gives no conclusion.

figure.alt: Graph of y=(x+3)(x−4). The roots are −3 and 4.
figure.caption: Roots are the x-values where the graph meets the x-axis, so y = 0.

blocks.title: Make one side zero
blocks.html: Move every term to one side and read the signed coefficients. For \(2x^2=3x+4\), subtract \(3x+4\) to get \(2x^2-3x-4=0\). Thus \(a=2\), \(b=-3\) and \(c=-4\).

blocks.title: Is there a common factor?
blocks.html: Take out the common factor before looking for two brackets.
Dividing \(3x^2=6x\) by \(x\) assumes \(x\ne0\) and loses the root \(0\). Take \(x\) out as a factor and check both factors.

blocks.hint: Take out \(2x\) after making one side zero.

retry.feedback: \(7\) is one root. Solve the factor \(2x=0\) as well.
\(0\) is one root. Solve \(x-7=0\) for the other.

blocks.title: How do I factorise when the leading coefficient is 1?
blocks.html:
For \(x^{2}+bx+c\), look for two numbers that add to \(b\) and multiply to \(c\). This comes from expanding:

\[(x+p)(x+q)=x^{2}+(p+q)x+pq.\]

For a negative product choose numbers with opposite signs. Use the sum to decide which is positive.

blocks.hint: Find a pair with product \(-15\) and sum \(2\).

retry.feedback: \(3\) is correct. The factor \(x+5\) gives another root.
\(-5\) is correct. The factor \(x-3\) gives another root.
These are the numbers in the brackets. Set each bracket equal to zero to find the roots.

blocks.title: How do I factorise when the leading coefficient differs from 1?
blocks.html:
1. Multiply \(a\) by \(c\).
  2. Find two numbers with product \(ac\) and sum \(b\).
  3. Split \(bx\) using these numbers.
  4. Factorise each pair of terms, then take out the shared bracket.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(2x^2+5x-3=0\) by splitting the middle term. Give all real roots.
blocks.hint: Look for two numbers with product \(-6\) and sum \(5\).
blocks.solution: Split \(5x\) as \(6x-x\) and group to get \((2x-1)(x+3)=0\). The roots are \(-3\) and \(\frac12\).

retry.feedback: Find the other root from \(2x-1=0\).
Find the other root from \(x+3=0\).
Check the sign of each root by setting its factor to zero.

blocks.html: Use your calculator to check your answer. Show the algebraic method and all necessary working. Follow any method specified in the question.

blocks.title: Useful factorisation patterns
blocks.html:
A difference of two squares

\[A^{2}-B^{2}=(A-B)(A+B).\]

Solve \(9x^{2}-16=0\). This becomes \((3x-4)(3x+4)=0\), giving \(x=\pm\frac{4}{3}\).

A repeated root

\[x^{2}-6x+9=(x-3)^{2}.\]

The equation \((x-3)^{2}=0\) has one distinct root, \(x=3\), called a repeated root.
If you cannot find simple factors, use the formula or complete the square. The equation may still have real roots.

sections.title: When should I use the formula or complete the square?
sections.label: Formula and completing the square
sections.intro: Both methods work with fractions and surds. Use the method specified in the question.

blocks.html:
For \(ax^2+bx+c=0\), with \(a\ne0\), use the signed coefficients.

\[x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}.\]

Divide the whole numerator by \(2a\). If the discriminant is positive, use both signs.

blocks.solution: \(x=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{20}}2=2\pm\sqrt5\).

blocks.html:
How many real roots?

The discriminant is \(D=b^{2}-4ac\), the number inside the square root.

  • \(D>0\): two distinct real roots.
  • \(D=0\): one repeated real root, \(x=\frac{-b}{2a}\).
  • \(D<0\): no real roots.

For example, \(x^{2}+2x+2=0\) has \(D=4-8=-4\), so it has no real solutions.

blocks.title: Solve by completing the square
blocks.html: When solving an equation, divide both sides by the non-zero leading coefficient if needed. When rewriting an expression, factor that coefficient out of the quadratic and linear terms. Then halve the coefficient of \(x\) inside the bracket and compensate for the square you add.
If an isolated real square equals a negative number, there are no real solutions. If it equals zero, there is just one value to recover.

blocks.title: Example with a leading coefficient other than 1
blocks.html:
Solve \(2x^{2}+12x+5=0\). First divide every term by 2.

\[x^{2}+6x+\frac{5}{2}=0\]

The leading coefficient is now 1.

\[(x+3)^{2}-9+\frac{5}{2}=0\]

Halve 6 to get 3. Subtract the added 9 to keep the expression equal.

\[(x+3)^{2}=\frac{13}{2}\]

Collect the constants.

\[x=-3\pm\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}\]

Take both square roots, simplify, and subtract 3.

sections.title: How can a substitution reveal a quadratic?
sections.label: Hidden quadratics and admissible values
sections.intro: Look for a repeated expression and its square. Solve for the substitute and then return to the original variable.

blocks.html: If \(u=x^2\), then \(u\ge0\). Reject negative values of \(u\). A positive value gives \(x=\pm\sqrt u\), while \(u=0\) gives only \(x=0\).

blocks.title: A quadratic in the square of x
blocks.html:
1. Choose the repeated expression.
  2. Write the possible values of the substitute.
  3. Solve the quadratic in the substitute.
  4. Find and check every permitted value of the original variable.

blocks.solution: The substitute values are \(3\) and \(-4\). Only \(3\) is allowed, giving \(x=\pm\sqrt3\).

retry.feedback: A positive square gives a positive root and a negative root.

blocks.title: What changes for a cube?
blocks.html:
Solve \(x^{6}-7x^{3}-8=0\). Use \(u=x^{3}\), because \(x^{6}=(x^{3})^{2}\). Here \(u\) may be any real number.

\[u^{2}-7u-8=(u-8)(u+1)=0\]

The substitute values are 8 and −1; both are allowed.

\[x^{3}=8\Rightarrow x=2\]

Take the real cube root.

\[x^{3}=-1\Rightarrow x=-1\]

A cube can be negative. Each branch has one real root.

Answer: \(x=-1\quad\text{or}\quad x=2\). Do not add a ± sign when taking a real cube root.

blocks.prompt: A substitution \(u=x^3\) gives \(u=-8\) or \(u=27\). Recover every real value of \(x\).
blocks.hint: A real cube root has the same sign as its input.

sections.title: How do I solve an equation containing a square root?
sections.label: Substitute for a square root
sections.intro: When \(x\) and \(\sqrt x\) both appear, set \(u=\sqrt x\) and replace \(x\) with \(u^2\).

blocks.html: Write \(x\ge0\) and \(u\ge0\). The real square root returns a non-negative number. Solve for \(u\), keep only allowed values and use \(x=u^2\).
Reject a negative value of \(u=\sqrt x\) before squaring it. Check candidates in the original equation because squaring can introduce extra answers.

blocks.solution: \(u=2\) or \(u=-3\). Keep \(2\), then \(x=2^2=4\). The original left side is \(4+2-6=0\).

retry.feedback: Check the discarded \(u=-3\). It cannot be the value of a real square root.

blocks.html:
Can both substituted roots be valid?

Yes. For \(x-5\sqrt{x}+6=0\), set \(u=\sqrt{x}\ge0\). Then \((u-2)(u-3)=0\). Both values are permitted, so \(x=4\) or \(x=9\).

sections.title: Which solutions satisfy the original problem?
sections.label: Fractions, reciprocals and valid roots
sections.intro: Write the restrictions before you change the equation. Test each candidate in the original equation or model.

blocks.html: Record any values that make an original denominator zero. Multiplying through or cancelling a factor does not remove those restrictions.

Clearing two denominators

Solve \(\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{2}{x+1}=1\). The original restrictions are \(x\ne1\) and \(x\ne-1\).

\[(x+1)+2(x-1)=(x-1)(x+1)\]

Multiply every term by the common denominator, which is nonzero for permitted values.

\[3x-1=x^{2}-1\]

Expand the brackets.

\[x(x-3)=0\]

Rearrange and factorise without dividing by x.

\[x=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=3\]

Both roots avoid the forbidden values and satisfy the original equation.

blocks.hint: Factorise the numerator and record the value excluded by the denominator.
blocks.solution: The numerator is \((x-3)(x+2)\). The original denominator excludes \(3\), so \(x=-2\) is the only root.

retry.feedback: The numerator is zero at both values. At \(3\) the denominator is zero, so discard \(3\).

blocks.title: Which terms repeat in a reciprocal equation?
blocks.html: If you see \(1/x\) and \(1/x^2\), try \(u=1/x\). Keep both \(x\ne0\) and \(u\ne0\), and return by \(x=1/u\).

blocks.solution: The factors are \((2u-1)(3u-1)\). Invert \(u=\frac12\) and \(u=\frac13\) to get \(x=2\) or \(x=3\).

blocks.title: Which root fits the model?
blocks.html: Translate the problem and record any conditions on lengths, time or other quantities.

blocks.title: Before you move on
blocks.html:
• Have you returned to the original variable?
  • Have you considered every factor and every permitted branch?
  • Have you retained denominator, square-root and model restrictions?
  • Have you checked candidates in the original equation after squaring or clearing denominators?
  • Have you given exact values unless approximations were requested?

sections.title: How do I use fractional powers and reciprocal sums?
sections.label: Fractional powers and reciprocal sums
sections.intro: Two longer applications use a real cube root or the whole sum \(x+\tfrac1x\) as the substitute.

blocks.html: Read \(x^{1/3}\) as the real cube root and \(x^{2/3}\) as its square. Both exist for negative inputs too.

blocks.hint: Factor the quadratic in \(u=\sqrt[3]{x}\). Then cube each value of \(u\).

blocks.title: Return from the reciprocal sum
blocks.html: For \(u=x+\tfrac1x\), record \(x\ne0\). Each candidate leads to \(x^2-ux+1=0\). Its discriminant tells you whether that value of \(u\) is possible.

blocks.solution: The substitute satisfies \((u-4)(u+1)=0\). Reject \(u=-1\). For \(u=4\), solve \(x^2-4x+1=0\) to obtain \(x=2\pm\sqrt3\).

glossary.definition: A value that makes the equation true.
The number multiplying a term, including its sign.
Write an expression as a product.
A root whose factor occurs more than once, as in \((x-3)^2=0\).
A condition on allowed values, such as \(x\ne0\) or \(x\ge0\).

  • Keep the original denominator and square-root restrictions. Check after squaring.

  • Keep exact values through your working. Give non-exact answers to 3 significant figures unless the question gives another accuracy.

examples.title: A coefficient greater than 1
examples.question: Solve \(2x^{2}+3=7x\).
solution:
Subtract \(7x\) to make one side zero.

\[2x^2-7x+3=0.\]

\[(-6)(-1)=6,\quad-6-1=-7\]

Find numbers with product \(ac=2\times3=6\) and sum \(b=-7\).

\[2x^{2}-6x-x+3=0\]

Split the middle term using those numbers.

\[2x(x-3)-(x-3)=0\]

Factorise each pair. Both contain \(x-3\).

\[(2x-1)(x-3)=0\]

Take out the shared bracket.

\[2x-1=0\text{ or }x-3=0\]

At least one factor must be zero. Consider both.

\[x=\frac{1}{2}\text{ or }x=3\]

Solve the linear equations. Both values satisfy the original equation.

examples.title: Keep exact answers
examples.question: Solve \(3x^{2}+2x-4=0\).
solution:
\[a=3,\quad b=2,\quad c=-4\]

Identify the signed coefficients.

\[x=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{2^{2}-4(3)(-4)}}{2(3)}\]

Substitute carefully. The negative constant is inside brackets.

\[x=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{52}}{6}\]

The number under the root is \(4+48=52\).

\[x=\frac{-2\pm2\sqrt{13}}{6}\]

Simplify the square root: \(\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}\).

\[x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{13}}{3}\]

Divide both terms of the numerator and the denominator by 2.

examples.title: Expose a square
examples.question: Solve \(x^{2}+6x+1=0\).
solution:
\[(x+3)^{2}-9+1=0\]

Expanding the square gives \(x^{2}+6x+9\), so subtract 9 to compensate.

\[(x+3)^{2}=8\]

Collect the constants and isolate the square.

\[x+3=\pm\sqrt{8}\]

Both a positive and a negative number can have square 8.

\[x=-3\pm2\sqrt{2}\]

Subtract 3 and simplify the surd.

examples.title: A quadratic in x²
examples.question: Find every real solution of \(x^{4}-13x^{2}+36=0\).
solution:
\[u=x^{2},\quad u\ge0\]

Since \(x^{4}=(x^{2})^{2}\), this substitution makes the highest power \(u^{2}\). A real square cannot be negative.

\[u^{2}-13u+36=0\]

Replace each occurrence of \(x^{2}\) consistently.

\[(u-4)(u-9)=0\]

Factorise: the numbers multiply to 36 and add to −13.

\[u=4\quad\text{or}\quad u=9\]

Both values satisfy \(u\ge0\).

\[x^{2}=4\Rightarrow x=\pm2\]

Return to \(x\). Both 2 and −2 have square 4.

\[x^{2}=9\Rightarrow x=\pm3\]

The second branch gives two more roots.
Complete answer: \(x=-3,-2,2,3\). For example, \(x=2\) gives \(16-52+36=0\). The negative root gives the same even powers.

examples.title: Reject an impossible square root
examples.question: Solve \(x-2\sqrt{x}-8=0\) for real \(x\).
solution:
\[u=\sqrt{x},\quad u\ge0\]

Record the restriction before solving.

\[u=4\Rightarrow x=4^{2}=16\]

Keep 4 and reject −2, since \(u\ge0\).

\[16-2\sqrt{16}-8=0\]

Check in the original equation.
The only real solution is \(x=16\). Squaring the rejected −2 would produce 4, but \(4-2\sqrt{4}-8=-8\), not zero.

examples.title: The only candidate is forbidden
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}=4\).
solution:
\[x\ne2\]

The original denominator must be nonzero.

\[\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=4\]

Factorise the numerator.

\[x+2=4\Rightarrow x=2\]

Cancellation is valid only for the permitted values \(x\ne2\).
No solution. The candidate 2 makes the original expression undefined. It must be rejected.

examples.title: A root that does not fit the model
examples.question: A rectangle has sides \(x\) cm and \(x+3\) cm, and area 28 cm². Lengths must be positive, so \(x>0\).
solution:
\[x(x+3)=28\]

Use length × width = area.

\[\begin{aligned}x^2+3x-28&=0\\ (x+7)(x-4)&=0.\end{aligned}\]

The algebra gives −7 or 4.

Reject −7 because it gives negative lengths. Keep \(x=4\): the sides are 4 cm and 7 cm, and their product is 28 cm². The rejected value is a valid root of the algebraic equation, but it is invalid for this situation.

examples.title: Rearrange and read the signs
examples.question: Write \(2x^2=3x+4\) in the form \(ax^2+bx+c=0\).
solution:
Subtract \(3x+4\) from both sides.

\[2x^2-3x-4=0.\]
The signed coefficients are \(a=2\), \(b=-3\), \(c=-4\). A missing term has coefficient zero.

examples.title: Keep the zero root
examples.question: Solve \(3x^2=6x\).
solution:
Make one side zero and take out the common factor.

\[3x^2-6x=3x(x-2)=0.\]
Either \(3x=0\) or \(x-2=0\). The two roots are \(0\) and \(2\).

examples.title: Choose the multiplier pair
examples.question: Solve \(x^2-x-12=0\). Find two numbers with sum \(-1\) and product \(-12\).
solution:
PairSum
1, −12−11
2, −6−4
3, −4−1 ✓
−3, 41

Use \(3\) and \(-4\). Expand the brackets to check.

\[(x+3)(x-4)=0.\]
Set each factor to zero. The roots are \(x=-3\) and \(x=4\).

examples.title: Use a reciprocal substitution
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{2}{x^2}-\frac{3}{x}+1=0\), where \(x\ne0\).
solution: Let \(u=1/x\). The first term is \(2u^2\), and \(u\ne0\).

Factorise the equation in \(u\).

\[\begin{aligned}2u^2-3u+1&=0\\ (2u-1)(u-1)&=0.\end{aligned}\]
Keep \(u=\frac12\) and \(u=1\). Return to \(x=\frac1u\), giving \(x=2\) or \(x=1\). Both satisfy the original equation.

examples.title: Use the real cube root
examples.question: Solve \(x^{2/3}-x^{1/3}-2=0\) for real \(x\).
solution: Let \(u=\sqrt[3]{x}\), so \(x^{2/3}=u^2\) and \(x=u^3\). A real cube root can be negative.
Cube each value to return to the original variable. The solutions are \(x=8\) and \(x=-1\).

examples.title: When the repeated expression is a sum
examples.question: Solve \(\left(x+\tfrac1x\right)^2-5\left(x+\tfrac1x\right)+6=0\), with \(x\ne0\).
solution: Set \(u=x+\tfrac1x\). Then \((u-2)(u-3)=0\), so test \(u=2\) and \(u=3\).
For \(u=2\), multiplying by the non-zero \(x\) gives \(x^2-2x+1=0\), so \(x=1\).
For \(u=3\), solve \(x^2-3x+1=0\). Its roots are \(\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\).
All three roots are non-zero. In general the return equation \(x^2-ux+1=0\) needs \(u^2-4\ge0\) for real \(x\). Thus \(|u|\ge2\).

orig_quadratics_completing_square.description: Complete the square to find a parabola’s vertex, exact roots and range on a restricted domain. Try worked examples and check your answers for 9709 Pure 1.

sections.title: How do I make a perfect square?
sections.label: Make the square
sections.intro: Rewrite the expression as \(a(x-h)^2+k\). Its value stays the same for every \(x\).

blocks.html: Expand \((x+p)^2=x^2+2px+p^2\). To match the \(x\) term, halve its coefficient. Subtract the constant the square adds.

figure.alt: Two strips of area 3x surround a square of area x squared. The hatched three-by-three corner completes a square of side x + 3.
figure.caption: For \(x>0\), the two strips contribute \(6x\). The hatched corner adds \(9\), so \(x^2+6x=(x+3)^2-9\). The identity holds for every real \(x\).

blocks.html: In \(x^2+6x+2\), the square adds \(9\). Subtract \(9\), then add the original \(2\). The outside constant is \(-7\).

blocks.prompt: Complete the step \(x^2+8x=(x+4)^2-\Box\). What belongs in the box?

retry.feedback: The number inside the bracket is 4. The constant it adds is the square of 4.

blocks.title: Further example with a fractional coefficient
blocks.html:
The same method applies. For \(x^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x-1\), halve \(\frac{3}{2}\) to get \(\frac{3}{4}\). Square this number exactly; do not round it.

\[(\frac{3}{4})^{2}=\frac{9}{16}\]

Square both the numerator and denominator.

\[x^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x-1=(x+\frac{3}{4})^{2}-\frac{9}{16}-1\]

Subtract the added square and include the original constant.

\[x^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x-1=(x+\frac{3}{4})^{2}-\frac{25}{16}\]

Write \(1=\frac{16}{16}\) before combining the constants.

A fractional answer is perfectly acceptable. Completed form does not require whole numbers inside or outside the bracket.
When the task says “complete the square”, give an equivalent expression. There is no need to set it equal to zero or find values of \(x\) unless an equation is also given.

sections.title: What if the leading coefficient is different from 1?
sections.label: Keep the outside multiplier
sections.intro: For an equation, you may divide both sides by \(a\ne0\). For an expression, factor \(a\) out of the quadratic and linear terms so the value stays the same.

blocks.html: Keep the original constant outside. The outside multiplier applies to both the squared bracket and the number subtracted inside it.
From \(3((x-2)^2-4)+5\), multiply \(-4\) by \(3\) before adding \(5\). The final constant is \(-7\).

blocks.hint: The \(9\) you subtract inside is multiplied by \(2\).

retry.feedback: This uses 5 − 9. Multiply the subtracted 9 by the outside coefficient 2.

blocks.title: Why the general identity works
blocks.html:
For \(a\ne0\), the same process gives

\[ax^{2}+bx+c=a(x+\frac{b}{2a})^{2}+c-\frac{b^{2}}{4a}.\]

After factoring out \(a\), the linear coefficient inside is \(\frac{b}{a}\). Halving it gives \(\frac{b}{2a}\). Its square is \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a^{2}}\), so the outside multiplier makes the constant correction \(-\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\).

The identity is a useful check. Applying the steps also helps you keep track of negative signs and fractions.

sections.title: Where is the vertex?
sections.label: Read the vertex and axis
sections.intro: Find the input that makes the squared bracket zero. Then read its output.

blocks.html: For \(y=a(x-h)^{2}+k\), the vertex or turning point is \((h,k)\), and the axis of symmetry is the vertical line \(x=h\).

figure.alt: The graph y=3(x−2)²−7 has vertex (2,−7) and a vertical symmetry axis x=2.
figure.caption: At x = h, the square is zero. Here h = 2 and k = −7.

blocks.html:
The square becomes zero at \(x=h\). Equal distances to either side of this value give the same square, so they give the same height on the graph.

For example, substituting \(x=h+1\) or \(x=h-1\) gives \(y=a+k\) in both cases. This explains why the vertical line through the vertex divides a parabola into two matching halves.

  • If \(a>0\), the parabola opens upwards. For all real \(x\), \(y\ge k\), so the minimum value is \(k\), reached at \(x=h\).
  • If \(a<0\), the parabola opens downwards. For all real \(x\), \(y\le k\), so the maximum value is \(k\), reached at \(x=h\).
Find the value that makes the bracket zero. In \((x+2)^{2}\), this is \(x=-2\). Also distinguish the extreme value, its location, and the vertex as a coordinate pair.

blocks.solution: The bracket is zero at \(x=-1\), so the vertex is \((-1,6)\).

retry.feedback: The bracket is \(x+1\). It is zero at \(x=-1\).

blocks.html: In the original form \(ax^{2}+bx+c\), the same result gives \(h=-\frac{b}{2a}\). Substitute this value into the expression to find \(k\). Completing the square explains this formula: the squared bracket is zero when \(x+\frac{b}{2a}=0\).

sections.title: How can I sketch the parabola?
sections.label: Sketch the graph
sections.intro: For \(f(x)=x^2-4x-5\), the vertex, symmetry line and intercepts fix the shape of the sketch.

blocks.html:
A reliable sketching sequence

  1. Use the sign of \(a\) to decide the opening direction.
  2. Mark the vertex and draw the vertical axis of symmetry.
  3. Set \(x=0\) to find the y-intercept.
  4. Set \(y=0\) to find any real x-intercepts.
  5. Draw a smooth, symmetric curve through the points. Label coordinates and show its continuing direction.

A sketch needs the correct shape and key coordinates; it does not need an exact scale. Factorising may be the quickest way to find the x-intercepts, even when completing the square was best for finding the vertex.

blocks.prompt: Read the two x-intercepts from the sketch of \(y=(x-2)^2-9\). Check them by setting \(y=0\).
blocks.hint: Set \(y=0\). Isolate the square and take both signs.
blocks.solution: \(x-2=\pm3\), so the intercepts are at \(x=-1\) and \(x=5\).

retry.feedback: This is the root from the positive square root. Use the negative square root too.

blocks.prompt: Now sketch \(y=(x+1)^2-4\) on paper. Give the x-values of both intercepts.
blocks.hint: Set \(y=0\). Which two values of \(x+1\) square to \(4\)?
blocks.solution: \(x+1=\pm2\), so \(x=-3\) or \(x=1\). The intercepts are equally far from the axis \(x=-1\).

retry.feedback: You have the right-hand intercept. Use \(x+1=-2\) for the other one.
You have the left-hand intercept. Use \(x+1=2\) for the other one.

blocks.html:
What if there are no two x-intercepts?

The equation \(a(x-h)^{2}+k=0\) becomes \((x-h)^{2}=-\frac{k}{a}\). A positive right-hand side gives two intercepts; zero gives one repeated root at the vertex; a negative right-hand side gives no real intercepts. For example, \(y=(x-2)^{2}+3\) stays above the x-axis.

blocks.title: Use the completed form to solve
blocks.html:
To solve \(x^2+6x+2=0\), rewrite the left side as \((x+3)^2-7\).

\[(x+3)^2=7,\qquad x=-3\pm\sqrt7.\]

The roots are the same distance from \(x=-3\). A square equal to zero gives one real root; a square equal to a negative number gives none.

blocks.title: How translations and stretches affect the sketch
blocks.html:
Build \(y=a(x-h)^{2}+k\) from \(y=x^{2}\): multiply the outputs by \(a\), then translate horizontally by \(h\) and vertically by \(k\).

  • \(h>0\) moves the vertex right; \(h<0\) moves it left. Thus \((x+2)^{2}\) has its vertex at \(x=-2\).
  • \(k>0\) moves the graph up; \(k<0\) moves it down.
  • \(|a|>1\) produces a vertical stretch and a narrower parabola. For \(0<|a|<1\), the parabola is wider.
  • A negative \(a\) also reflects the scaled graph in the x-axis before the translations, so the final parabola opens downwards.
Read the bracket carefully. The vertex occurs where the squared bracket is zero. The coefficient \(a\) controls the shape; it is not a constant gradient. A parabola's gradient changes along the curve.

sections.title: What outputs can the parabola take?
sections.label: Find the range
sections.intro: The domain gives the allowed inputs. The range gives every output reached by those inputs.

blocks.html:
For every real \(x\), \((x-h)^{2}\ge0\), with equality at \(x=h\). Use the sign of \(a\) to decide whether \(k\) is a minimum or a maximum.

Write the range as an inequality in the output or as an interval. For instance, \(f(x)\ge-7\), \(y\ge-7\) and \([-7,\infty)\) describe the same outputs. The input is \(x\).

blocks.prompt: Find the range of \(f(x)=-3(x-1)^2+8\) for all real \(x\).
blocks.hint: The parabola opens downwards. Is the vertex included?
blocks.solution: The greatest output is \(8\), reached at \(x=1\). Write \(f(x)\le8\), \(y\le8\) or \((-\infty,8]\).

retry.feedback: The leading coefficient is negative. Values go down from the vertex.

blocks.html:
Why these are complete ranges

As \(x\) varies over all real numbers, \((x-h)^{2}\) takes every nonnegative value. Therefore an upward-opening quadratic takes every output from its minimum upwards; a downward-opening quadratic takes every output from its maximum downwards. There are no gaps.

Consequently, \(y=a(x-h)^{2}+k\) has range \([k,\infty)\) when \(a>0\), and \((-\infty,k]\) when \(a<0\), provided the domain is all real numbers.

Use interval brackets accurately. A square bracket includes an attained endpoint; a round bracket excludes it. Infinity is never an attained value, so always use a round bracket beside \(\infty\) or \(-\infty\).

sections.title: How does a restricted domain change the range?
sections.label: Check a closed interval
sections.intro: On a closed interval, compare the two endpoint outputs and the vertex output if its input belongs to the interval.

blocks.html: For a closed interval: calculate the outputs at both endpoints and at the vertex, if it lies inside the interval. The smallest of these outputs is the minimum; the largest is the maximum. This works for either opening direction.

blocks.solution: The vertex gives \(0\). The endpoint outputs are \(9\) and \(4\). The range is \(0\le g(x)\le9\), or \([0,9]\).

retry.feedback: Compare both endpoint values. The left endpoint is farther from the vertex.

blocks.title: A maximum inside a closed interval
blocks.html: For \(g(x)=-2(x-1)^{2}+8\) on \([-1,4]\), the included vertex gives \(g(1)=8\), the maximum. The endpoints give \(g(-1)=0\) and \(g(4)=-10\). Therefore the range is \([-10,8]\).

sections.title: What changes at an open boundary?
sections.label: Open and unbounded domains
sections.intro: Follow the allowed part of the curve. A boundary output can be approached, attained at another input, or both.

blocks.html: At an open end, check whether another allowed input gives the same output. At an unbounded end, follow the graph as the input continues.

blocks.hint: The interval starts to the right of the vertex. Which output does the curve approach as \(x\) approaches \(-1\) from the right?
blocks.solution: For every permitted input, \(x+2>1\). Its square takes every value greater than \(1\). The range is \(h(x)>1\), or \((1,\infty)\).

retry.feedback: The boundary \(x=-1\) is excluded. The other input with output \(1\), namely \(x=-3\), is outside the domain too.

blocks.html:
For an open boundary, calculate the output the curve approaches there, then ask whether another permitted input gives that same output. For an unbounded domain, also inspect what happens as the input continues indefinitely in the allowed direction. Do not assume a function has both an attained minimum and an attained maximum.

Open endpoints: check whether the output is attained elsewhere

Consider \(q(x)=(x-1)^{2}\).

  • For \(0<x\le2\), the range is \([0,1]\). The vertex gives 0, and the included input 2 gives 1. Excluding input 0 does not exclude output 1.
  • For \(0<x<2\), the range is \([0,1)\). The output approaches 1 at both ends, but neither input producing 1 is permitted.
  • For \(x>1\), the range is \((0,\infty)\). Outputs can be arbitrarily close to zero, but zero is never attained.
Domain brackets do not transfer automatically to the range. An output is included whenever at least one permitted input produces it.

Show the restriction on your sketch

Draw only the permitted part of the parabola. Use a filled endpoint for an included input and a hollow endpoint for an excluded input. Keep an arrow where the allowed curve continues indefinitely. An endpoint marker describes that particular point; a different included point may still produce the same output.

blocks.title: Modelling the area of a rectangle
blocks.html:
A rectangle has perimeter 20 cm. If one side is \(x\) cm, the other is \(10-x\) cm. Both lengths must be positive, so \(0<x<10\).

\[A=x(10-x)=25-(x-5)^{2}\]

The maximum area is 25 cm², attained at \(x=5\).

The rectangle is then a 5 cm by 5 cm square. Its area approaches zero as a side approaches zero, but zero area is excluded by the positive-length domain. Thus \(0<A\le25\). Whether a boundary is included comes from the stated model.

blocks.title: Before you move on
blocks.html:
• Have you read the horizontal shift with the correct sign?
  • Have you distinguished the extreme value, its input, and the vertex coordinates?
  • Have you used the stated domain and checked the vertex and relevant boundaries?
  • Have you included a range endpoint only when some allowed input attains it?
  • Does your sketch agree with the opening direction, intercepts and range?

glossary.definition: A multiple of a square plus a constant, \(a(x-h)^2+k\).
The turning point of the parabola.
The line through the vertex that divides the parabola into mirror images.
The allowed inputs.
The set of outputs the function takes.

revision.body:
Build the completed form

For \(a\ne0\), factor \(a\) out of the quadratic and linear terms, halve the new linear coefficient and subtract its square inside the bracket.

\[ax^2+bx+c=a(x+\tfrac{b}{2a})^2+c-\tfrac{b^2}{4a}.\]

Example: \(3x^2-12x+5=3((x-2)^2-4)+5=3(x-2)^2-7\).

Vertex, axis and sketch

In \(y=a(x-h)^2+k\), the vertex is \((h,k)\) and the symmetry line is \(x=h\). The bracket \(x+2\) is zero at \(-2\).

Use the sign of \(a\), mark the vertex and intercepts, then sketch. For the y-intercept use \(x=0\). For the x-intercepts solve \((x-h)^2=-k/a\). Its right side gives two, one or no real roots as it is positive, zero or negative.

Find the range

DomainWhat to check
All real x\(y\ge k\) or \([k,\infty)\) upwards. \(y\le k\) or \((-\infty,k]\) downwards.
Closed intervalCompare both endpoint outputs and the allowed vertex output.
Open or unboundedCheck the limiting outputs. Include a bound if any allowed input attains it.

For \(q(x)=(x-1)^2\) on \(0<x\le2\), the range is \([0,1]\). Although \(x=0\) is excluded, \(x=2\) still gives \(1\).
revision.checks:
• Keep the outside multiplier on every term inside its bracket.
  • Separate the extreme value \(k\), its location \(h\) and the point \((h,k)\).
  • Expand to check the completed form. State which outputs are attained.
revision.examTip:
• Show the required method and all working. Use your calculator to check.
  • Keep exact values through your working. Give non-exact answers to 3 significant figures unless the question gives another accuracy.

examples.title: A positive linear coefficient
examples.question: Write \(x^{2}+6x+2\) in completed form.
solution:
\[\frac{6}{2}=3\]

Halve the coefficient of \(x\). This gives the number inside the bracket.

\[(x+3)^{2}=x^{2}+6x+9\]

Expanding the square shows the extra constant: 9.

\[x^{2}+6x=(x+3)^{2}-9\]

Subtract 9 to compensate. The two expressions are equal for every \(x\).

\[x^{2}+6x+2=(x+3)^{2}-7\]

Include the original constant: \(-9+2=-7\).

examples.title: A negative coefficient and a fraction
examples.question: Write \(x^{2}-5x+1\) in completed form.
solution:
\[\frac{-5}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}\]

Halve the signed coefficient. The bracket must contain a minus sign.

\[(x-\frac{5}{2})^{2}=x^{2}-5x+\frac{25}{4}\]

The constant created by squaring is positive, even though the number inside the bracket is negative.

\[x^{2}-5x+1=(x-\frac{5}{2})^{2}-\frac{25}{4}+1\]

Subtract the added square, then restore the original constant.

\[x^{2}-5x+1=(x-\frac{5}{2})^{2}-\frac{21}{4}\]

Use \(1=\frac{4}{4}\) to combine the constants exactly.

examples.title: Keep the outside multiplier
examples.question: Write \(3x^{2}-12x+5\) in completed form.
solution:
\[3x^{2}-12x+5=3(x^{2}-4x)+5\]

Factor 3 from the first two terms. Leave the constant 5 outside.

\[x^{2}-4x=(x-2)^{2}-4\]

Inside the bracket, halve −4 to get −2, then subtract its square.

\[3((x-2)^{2}-4)+5\]

The outside 3 multiplies both the square and the constant you subtracted.

\[3(x-2)^{2}-12+5\]

Multiply the constant you subtracted: \(3\times(-4)=-12\).

\[3x^{2}-12x+5=3(x-2)^{2}-7\]

Collect the constants and state the completed form.

examples.title: A negative leading coefficient
examples.question: Write \(-2x^{2}-8x+1\) in completed form.
solution:
\[\begin{aligned}-2x^2-8x+1\\ ={}-2(x^2+4x)+1.\end{aligned}\]

Factor out −2. The linear term inside becomes positive.

\[-2(x+2)^{2}+8+1\]

The constant you subtracted becomes positive because \((-2)(-4)=8\).

\[-2x^{2}-8x+1=-2(x+2)^{2}+9\]

Collect the constants. Expanding again checks both signs.

examples.title: Build an equation from the graph
examples.question: A parabola has vertex \((2,-3)\) and passes through \((0,5)\). Find its equation.
solution:
\[y=a(x-2)^{2}-3\]

The vertex supplies the bracket shift and the final constant. The coefficient \(a\) is still unknown.

\[5=a(0-2)^{2}-3\]

Substitute both coordinates of the other point.

\[5=4a-3\Rightarrow a=2\]

Solve for the missing coefficient.

\[y=2(x-2)^{2}-3\]

The equation has the required vertex and gives \(y=5\) when \(x=0\).

examples.title: Combine the useful forms
examples.question: Find the vertex and intercepts of \(f(x)=x^2-4x-5\) to explain the sketch above.
solution:
\[f(x)=(x-2)^{2}-9\]

Complete the square to reveal the vertex \((2,-9)\) and axis \(x=2\). The positive leading coefficient means the curve opens upwards.

\[f(0)=-5\]

The y-intercept is \((0,-5)\).

\[\frac{-1+5}{2}=2\]

The roots lie equally far from the axis, which checks the symmetry.
Draw the vertex below both intercepts and let both ends rise. The symmetry also gives the point \((4,-5)\) from \((0,-5)\).

examples.title: A minimum value
examples.question: Find the range of \(f(x)=3(x-2)^2-7\) for all real \(x\).
solution:
\[f(x)=3(x-2)^{2}-7\]

The domain is all real numbers. The squared term is smallest at \(x=2\).

\[3(x-2)^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow f(x)\ge-7\]

The minimum output is −7, and it is attained.
Range: \([-7,\infty)\), equivalently \(f(x)\ge-7\). The minimum value is −7; the input where it occurs is 2; the vertex is \((2,-7)\).

examples.title: A maximum value
examples.question: Find the range of \(g(x)=-2(x+2)^2+9\) for all real \(x\).
solution:
\[g(x)=-2(x+2)^{2}+9\]

The domain is all real numbers. A nonnegative square multiplied by −2 is nonpositive.

\[-2(x+2)^{2}\le0\Rightarrow g(x)\le9\]

The maximum is 9, attained when \(x=-2\).
The range is \(g(x)\le9\), equivalently \((-\infty,9]\). The outputs decrease without bound.

examples.title: A closed interval containing the vertex
examples.question: Find the range of \(f(x)=(x-2)^{2}-3\) for \(-1\le x\le4\).
solution:
\[f(2)=-3\]

The vertex input 2 is included, so −3 is the minimum.

\[f(-1)=6,\quad f(4)=1\]

The greatest distance from 2 occurs at −1, giving the maximum 6.
The range is \(-3\le f(x)\le6\), or \([-3,6]\). Both extrema are attained. Checking only the endpoints would miss the minimum.

examples.title: The vertex is outside the domain
examples.question: Find the range of \(f(x)=(x-2)^2-3\) for \(x\ge4\).
solution:
\[f(4)=1\]

The closest permitted input to 2 is 4. Beyond 4, the square increases without bound.
Range: \([1,\infty)\). The unrestricted minimum −3 is unavailable.

examples.title: Read the vertex and axis
examples.question: For \(y=3(x-2)^2-7\), give the vertex, axis and least value.
solution: Set the bracket equal to zero. \(x-2=0\) gives \(x=2\).
At \(x=2\), the squared term vanishes and \(y=-7\). The vertex is \((2,-7)\) and the axis is \(x=2\).
The coefficient \(3\) is positive, so all other outputs exceed \(-7\). The least value is \(-7\), reached at \(x=2\).

orig_quadratics_roots.description: Use the discriminant to count real roots, find parameter values and test for tangency. Explore repeated roots and exceptional cases with 9709 Pure 1 examples.

sections.title: What does the discriminant tell me?
sections.label: Count the real roots
sections.intro: Use the sign of the expression under the square root to count distinct real roots.

blocks.html: For \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) with \(a\ne0\), the discriminant is \(D=b^2-4ac\). The formula has \(\sqrt D\) in its numerator.

figure.alt: Three parabolas. The first meets the x-axis twice, the second touches it once, the third is above it.
figure.caption: Positive, zero and negative discriminants give two, one and no distinct real roots.

blocks.html:
ConditionReal solutionsGraph of the quadratic
\(D>0\)Two distinct real rootsCrosses the x-axis twice
\(D=0\)One distinct real root, repeated twiceTouches the x-axis at its vertex
\(D<0\)No real rootsDoes not meet the x-axis

blocks.prompt: How many distinct real roots does \(9x^2+6x+1=0\) have?
blocks.solution: \(D=0\). The root \(-\frac13\) is repeated, so there is one distinct root.

retry.feedback: The two signs give the same value when the discriminant is zero.

blocks.html:
Why the three cases work

If \(D>0\), the positive number \(\sqrt{D}\) gives two different numerators, \(-b+\sqrt{D}\) and \(-b-\sqrt{D}\). Dividing by the same nonzero number preserves two different answers.

If \(D=0\), the plus and minus versions coincide. The repeated root is \(x=-\frac{b}{2a}\). It counts as one distinct solution, even though its factor appears twice.

If \(D<0\), the square root is not real, so neither solution is real. Write “no real roots”; the qualification matters when complex numbers are being considered elsewhere.
Read the wording carefully. “Has real roots” allows a repeated root, so use \(D\ge0\). “Has two distinct real roots” requires \(D>0\). For a quadratic, “equal roots” means \(D=0\).
The discriminant counts real roots over all real \(x\). If a question restricts the domain, asks for positive roots, or comes from an equation with excluded values, check those conditions separately.

blocks.title: Connect the discriminant to the vertex
blocks.html:
The completed form can be written as

\[ax^{2}+bx+c=a(x+\frac{b}{2a})^{2}-\frac{D}{4a}.\]

The vertex output is therefore \(-\frac{D}{4a}\). If \(D=0\), the vertex is on the x-axis. If \(D>0\), the vertex is on the opposite side of the axis from the direction in which the arms extend, producing two crossings. If \(D<0\), the graph stays on one side of the axis.

This explains why the same root-count table works for both upward and downward parabolas.

sections.title: How do I calculate the discriminant accurately?
sections.label: Use signed coefficients
sections.intro: Make one side zero, then substitute the signed coefficients into the formula.

blocks.html: For example, \(2x^{2}=5x-1\) becomes \(2x^{2}-5x+1=0\), so the coefficients are \(2,-5,1\). A missing linear term means \(b=0\); a missing constant means \(c=0\).

retry.feedback: The constant is −3 after rearranging. Subtract the negative product.

blocks.html: A discriminant is a number, not a root. State its sign and the conclusion. If the question only asks how many real roots there are, calculating the roots is unnecessary.

blocks.title: When are real roots rational?
blocks.html:
For integer coefficients with \(a\ne0\), a non-negative perfect-square discriminant gives rational roots. A positive discriminant that is not a perfect square gives irrational roots. For example, \(D=28\) for \(3x^2+2x-2=0\) gives irrational roots.

With rational coefficients, first clear denominators to obtain integer coefficients. Do not apply the integer perfect-square test directly to an arbitrary fractional discriminant.

sections.title: Which parameter values give the required roots?
sections.label: Solve for the parameter
sections.intro: Check that the equation is quadratic and turn the required root count into a condition on D.

blocks.html: Two distinct real roots need \(D>0\). A real root is allowed when \(D=0\), so “has real roots” needs \(D\ge0\). Apply these tests where \(a\ne0\).

blocks.title: A sign check for a quadratic condition
blocks.html: When \(D\) is quadratic in the parameter, solve \(D=0\) for its boundaries. For \((k-2)(k+2)\), the signs to the left, between and to the right of \(-2\) and \(2\) are \(+\), \(−\), \(+\). Hence \(k^2-4>0\) outside the two roots. Include the roots only for \(\ge0\).
In \(x^2+2kx+2k^2-9=0\), the values \(k=-3\) and \(k=3\) give a repeated root. Exclude them if the question asks for two distinct real roots.

blocks.prompt: Find all \(k\) for which \(x^2-2kx+4=0\) has two distinct real roots.
blocks.hint: \(D=4(k^2-4)\). Decide where the product \((k-2)(k+2)\) is positive.
blocks.solution: \(D>0\) gives \(k<-2\) or \(k>2\). The endpoints produce a repeated root.

retry.feedback: Try k = 0. The discriminant is negative between the two boundaries.
Strict positivity excludes the values that make D zero.

blocks.html: The symbol \(\cup\) means “union”: values in either interval are allowed. Round brackets exclude a boundary; square brackets include it. Infinity always takes a round bracket.

sections.title: What happens when the square term disappears?
sections.label: Check the linear or constant case
sections.intro: Find which parameters make the leading coefficient zero. Substitute those values in the original equation.

blocks.html: Separate the exceptional values before using the quadratic rule. A positive discriminant calculated from the coefficients does not guarantee two solutions when \(a=0\). The equation is no longer quadratic, and the denominator \(2a\) in the quadratic formula is zero.

Three possibilities when the square term disappears

What remainsConclusion
\(bx+c=0,\quad b\ne0\)One solution: \(x=-\frac{c}{b}\).
A nonzero constant equal to zero, such as \(5=0\)An impossible statement: no solutions.
\(0=0\)An identity: every real \(x\) is a solution, provided the original domain allows it.

In the last two rows, both the quadratic and linear coefficients are zero. An equation with no variable term still needs interpreting; it does not automatically have one solution.

blocks.hint: The coefficient of \(x^2\) is zero. What equation remains?

blocks.title: Constant equations
blocks.html:
In \((u-1)x^{2}+(u-1)x+2=0\), setting \(u=1\) leaves \(2=0\). No input can satisfy this equation. In \((u-1)(x^{2}+x+2)=0\), the same parameter value leaves \(0=0\), which every real input satisfies.

Although both equations lose their variable terms at the exceptional value, their conclusions are opposite. Evaluate all the coefficients, including the constant. Dividing the second equation by \(u-1\) would lose its entire all-real solution case.

Do not divide away an exceptional case. Dividing by an expression such as \(t-2\) assumes it is nonzero. Record and check the zero case first, then combine it with the other cases in your final answer.

sections.title: When does a line touch a parabola?
sections.label: Find a tangent and contact point
sections.intro: Make the curve and line outputs equal. Tangency occurs when this quadratic has a repeated root.

blocks.html: Use the discriminant of the intersection equation. Two distinct real roots mean two intersection points; a repeated root means the line is tangent to the parabola; no real roots mean there are no intersection points. These conclusions assume the whole line and parabola are available.

Crossing, touching and missing

For the parabola \(y=x^2-4x+5\) and the horizontal line \(y=c\), the intersection equation is \(x^2-4x+5-c=0\). Its discriminant is \(4(c-1)\). Compare \(c=3\), \(c=1\) and \(c=-1\).

The discriminant of the parabola's equation \(y=f(x)\) describes its intersections with the x-axis. It does not by itself decide its intersections with another line. For \(y=mx+c\), the relevant equation is \(f(x)-mx-c=0\).

blocks.solution: The discriminant is \(4c\), so \(c=0\). The line touches the curve at \((1,2)\).

blocks.html: A repeated root is an x-coordinate, not a complete point. Recover the y-coordinate from an original equation. If either graph has a restricted domain, check that the contact or intersection points lie in its permitted part.

blocks.title: Why a repeated root means tangency
blocks.html:
When the intersection equation has a repeated root \(x=r\), the difference between the curve's output and the line's output has the form \(a(x-r)^{2}\). This difference is zero at one input and keeps the same sign on both sides. The curve therefore meets the line without passing from one side of it to the other.

This also explains why a tangent need not be horizontal or pass through the vertex. The repeated root comes from the difference between the two graphs, rather than from the parabola alone.

sections.title: How can I show the sign for every real input?
sections.label: Sign of the whole parabola
sections.intro: Combine the opening direction with the number of points where the parabola meets the x-axis.

blocks.html:
A quadratic with no real roots never reaches the x-axis. It may stay entirely above it or entirely below it: the leading coefficient decides which. For example, \(x^{2}+1\) is always positive, whereas \(-x^{2}-1\) is always negative. Both have negative discriminants.

Required for every real xConditions for a quadratic
\(ax^{2}+bx+c>0\)\(a>0\) and \(\Delta<0\)
\(ax^{2}+bx+c\ge0\)\(a>0\) and \(\Delta\le0\)
\(ax^{2}+bx+c<0\)\(a<0\) and \(\Delta<0\)
\(ax^{2}+bx+c\le0\)\(a<0\) and \(\Delta\le0\)
Strict inequalities exclude contact with the x-axis. Allow \(\Delta=0\) only when zero outputs are permitted. A nonzero quadratic cannot be strictly positive or strictly negative at a real root.

blocks.prompt: Find all \(k\) such that \(2x^2+8x+k>0\) for every real \(x\).
blocks.hint: The parabola opens upwards. For strict positivity require \(D<0\).
blocks.solution: \(64-8k<0\), so \(k>8\). At \(k=8\) the minimum is zero.

retry.feedback: Allowing k = 8 would include a minimum of zero. The question requires a positive value.

blocks.html: These conditions agree with completing the square: the vertex output is \(-\frac{\Delta}{4a}\). An upward parabola must have a positive minimum to be strictly positive everywhere; a downward parabola must have a negative maximum to be strictly negative everywhere.

blocks.title: Exceptional constant cases and restricted domains
blocks.html:
Include any constant case separately

If \(a=0\) but \(b\ne0\), the linear expression takes both positive and negative values as \(x\) varies over all real numbers. It cannot satisfy any row of the table for every input. If \(a=b=0\), the expression is constant: simply check the required sign of \(c\). The zero constant is both nonnegative and nonpositive, but it satisfies neither strict inequality.

“For every real x” matters. On a restricted domain, a quadratic can stay positive even when it has real roots elsewhere. Use the permitted inputs and minimum or maximum on that domain instead of applying the all-real conditions unchanged.

blocks.title: Before you move on
blocks.html:
• Have you formed the correct equation and used signed coefficients?
  • Have you checked every parameter value that removes the square term?
  • Does your discriminant condition match “real”, “distinct”, “equal”, or “tangent”?
  • For positivity or negativity, have you also checked the leading coefficient?
  • Have you included the correct boundaries and answered in the requested parameter or coordinates?

glossary.definition: The expression \(b^2-4ac\) that determines the real-root count.
A fixed number within one equation that varies between cases.
Different values of the unknown.
A line with the same gradient as the curve at the contact point.

revision.body:
Form the equation and calculate \(D\)

Write \(ax^2+bx+c=0\). Check \(a\ne0\), then use signed coefficients in \(D=b^2-4ac\).

WordingConditionConclusion
Two distinct real roots\(D>0\)Two crossings.
Equal roots\(D=0\)One distinct root at \(x=\frac{-b}{2a}\).
No real roots\(D<0\)The graph misses the x-axis.
Has real roots\(D\ge0\)Includes a repeated root.

Parameters and tangency

  1. Deal separately with each parameter that makes \(a=0\). Substitute it in the original equation. A remaining constant statement can be true for all inputs or false for all inputs.
  2. Use the condition on \(D\). Solve for the parameter and test intervals if \(D\) is quadratic.
  3. For tangency solve \(f(x)=mx+c\), set the discriminant of that equation to zero and recover the contact point using either original equation.

One sign for every real input

For strict positivity use \(a>0\) and \(D<0\). For strict negativity use \(a<0\) and \(D<0\). If zero is allowed, change to \(D\le0\). Check any linear or constant case separately.
revision.checks: Show the discriminant condition and the correct endpoints. Check restrictions on \(x\) after counting the roots of an unrestricted quadratic.
revision.examTip:
• Show the required method and all working. Use your calculator to check.
  • Keep exact values through your working. Give non-exact answers to 3 significant figures unless the question gives another accuracy.

examples.title: Two distinct real roots
examples.question: Determine the nature of the roots of \(3x^{2}+2x-2=0\), then find them exactly.
solution:
\[a=3,\quad b=2,\quad c=-2\]

The constant coefficient is negative.

\[D=2^{2}-4(3)(-2)=28\]

Subtracting a negative product adds 24.

\[D>0\]

There are two distinct real roots. This answers the “nature of the roots” part.

\[x=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{28}}{6}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{7}}{3}\]

Use the quadratic formula and simplify the surd. Keep exact values.

examples.title: A repeated root
examples.question: Classify and solve \(4x^{2}-12x+9=0\).
solution:
\[D=(-12)^{2}-4(4)(9)=0\]

Square the signed coefficient. The square of −12 is positive 144.

\[x=-\frac{-12}{2(4)}=\frac{3}{2}\]

The two formula branches coincide: one distinct real solution.

\[4x^{2}-12x+9=(2x-3)^{2}\]

The repeated factor confirms the result. The graph touches the x-axis at \((\frac{3}{2},0)\).

examples.title: No real roots
examples.question: Determine the nature of the roots of \(x^{2}+4x+7=0\).
solution:
\[D=4^{2}-4(1)(7)=-12\]

The discriminant is negative, so there are no real roots.

\[x^{2}+4x+7=(x+2)^{2}+3\]

The completed form confirms that the expression is always at least 3, so it cannot equal zero.

examples.title: A linear condition in the parameter
examples.question: Find all \(k\) for which \(x^{2}-8x+k=0\) has real roots.
solution:
\[D=(-8)^{2}-4(1)(k)=64-4k\]

The leading coefficient is always 1, so the equation remains quadratic.

\[64-4k\ge0\]

“Real roots” includes the repeated-root boundary.

\[-4k\ge-64\Rightarrow k\le16\]

Dividing by −4 reverses the inequality sign.

\[k\in(-\infty,16]\]

Include 16 because it gives \((x-4)^{2}=0\). For two distinct roots, the answer would instead be \(k<16\).

examples.title: An interval between two boundaries
examples.question: Find all \(k\) for which \(x^{2}+2kx+2k^{2}-9=0\) has two distinct real roots.
solution:
\[\begin{aligned}D&=(2k)^2-4(2k^2-9)\\&=36-4k^2.\end{aligned}\]

The entire constant coefficient is \(2k^{2}-9\). Keep it in brackets.

\[36-4k^{2}>0\Rightarrow k^{2}<9\]

Use a strict inequality because the roots must be distinct.

\[-3<k<3\]

A square is less than 9 when the original number lies between −3 and 3.

examples.title: Two outside intervals with exact endpoints
examples.question: Find all \(k\) for which \(x^{2}-2kx+3k+2=0\) has real roots.
solution:
\[\begin{aligned}D&=(-2k)^2-4(3k+2)\\&=4(k^2-3k-2).\end{aligned}\]

Expand carefully, then remove the positive factor 4 when studying the sign.

\[k^{2}-3k-2\ge0\]

This is an inequality in \(k\), not in \(x\).

\[k^{2}-3k-2=0\Rightarrow k=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}\]

Find the two boundary values exactly using the quadratic formula.

\[k\le\frac{3-\sqrt{17}}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad k\ge\frac{3+\sqrt{17}}{2}\]

The quadratic in \(k\) opens upwards. It is non-negative outside the two boundary values, including both endpoints.

examples.title: Classify a whole family
examples.question: Determine the number of real solutions of \((t-2)x^{2}+2x+t-2=0\) for every real value of \(t\).
solution:
\[t=2\Rightarrow 2x=0\Rightarrow x=0\]

The square term vanishes at \(t=2\). This exceptional case has exactly one solution because the remaining equation is linear.

\[\Delta=2^{2}-4(t-2)(t-2)\]

For \(t\ne2\), the equation is quadratic. Use its signed coefficients.

\[\begin{aligned}\Delta&=4(1-(t-2)^2)\\&=4(3-t)(t-1).\end{aligned}\]

The discriminant is positive between 1 and 3, zero at the boundaries, and negative outside them.

Parameter valuesReal solutions
\(1<t<2\) or \(2<t<3\)Two distinct solutions.
\(t=1\) or \(t=3\)One repeated quadratic root: respectively \(x=1\) or \(x=-1\).
\(t=2\)One linear solution: \(x=0\).
\(t<1\) or \(t>3\)No real solutions.
Thus “exactly one real solution” gives \(t=1,2,3\), while “equal roots of a quadratic” gives only \(t=1\) or \(t=3\). Read the wording carefully.

examples.title: Find the intercept and contact point
examples.question: Find \(q\) so that \(y=3x+q\) is tangent to \(y=2x^{2}-x+5\). Find the point of contact.
solution:
\[2x^{2}-x+5=3x+q\]

Equate the two expressions for the same output.

\[2x^{2}-4x+5-q=0\]

The intersection equation has \(a=2\), \(b=-4\) and \(c=5-q\).

\[\Delta=16-8(5-q)=8q-24=0\]

Tangency requires a repeated root. Therefore \(q=3\).

\[\begin{gathered}x=-\frac{-4}{2\times2}=1,\\y=3(1)+3=6.\end{gathered}\]

Find the repeated root, then substitute into either original equation. The contact point is \((1,6)\).
Check: with \(q=3\), the intersection equation is \(2(x-1)^{2}=0\), and both graphs give \(y=6\) at \(x=1\). When \(q>3\) there are two intersections; when \(q<3\) there are none.

examples.title: Two possible tangent gradients
examples.question: Find the lines through \((0,-4)\) that are tangent to \(y=x^{2}\).
solution:
\[y=mx-4,\quad x^{2}-mx+4=0\]

A line of gradient \(m\) through the given point has intercept −4. Equating it to the parabola gives the intersection equation.

\[\Delta=m^{2}-16=0\Rightarrow m=\pm4\]

Both values are allowed. A squared parameter can produce two different tangents.

\[x=\frac{m}{2},\quad y=x^{2}=4\]

The contact points are \((2,4)\) when \(m=4\) and \((-2,4)\) when \(m=-4\).
Tangent equations: \(y=4x-4\) and \(y=-4x-4\). Both pass through the required point.

examples.title: Strict positivity
examples.question: Find all \(p\) for which \(3x^{2}-12x+p>0\) for every real \(x\).
solution:
\[a=3>0,\quad \Delta=144-12p\]

The graph already opens upwards. Its discriminant must be strictly negative.

\[144-12p<0\Rightarrow p>12\]

Rearrange to \(144<12p\), or reverse the inequality if dividing by −12.
Check: \(3x^{2}-12x+p=3(x-2)^{2}+p-12\). At \(p=12\), the minimum is zero, so this endpoint is excluded. For a nonnegative requirement instead, the answer would be \(p\ge12\).

examples.title: A valid exceptional constant
examples.question: Find all \(k\) such that \((k-1)x^{2}+2(k-1)x+4>0\) for every real \(x\).
solution:
\[k=1\Rightarrow f(x)=4>0\]

The exceptional value gives a positive constant. Keep \(k=1\).

\[k\ne1:\quad a=k-1>0\Rightarrow k>1\]

For the genuinely quadratic cases, the leading coefficient must be positive.

\[\begin{aligned}\Delta&=4(k-1)^2-16(k-1)\\&=4(k-1)(k-5).\end{aligned}\]

Now apply the strict discriminant condition as well.

\[\Delta<0\Rightarrow 1<k<5\]

This interval already satisfies \(k>1\). Combine it with the separately checked constant case.
Complete answer: \(1\le k<5\). At \(k=5\), the expression is \(4(x+1)^{2}\), which is zero at \(x=-1\); strict positivity fails.

orig_quadratics_inequalities.description: Solve quadratic inequalities using graphs and sign charts. Practise strict endpoints, repeated roots and intersecting constraints for 9709 Pure 1.

sections.title: What does an inequality ask me to find?
sections.label: Read and write intervals
sections.intro: Find every input for which the comparison is true. Start by deciding whether equality is allowed.

blocks.html:
For \(f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c\), with \(a\ne0\), the inequality \(f(x)>0\) asks where the graph is above the x-axis. The inequality \(f(x)<0\) asks where it is below the axis.

The answer consists of x-values. The roots of \(f(x)=0\) locate possible boundaries; they are not usually the complete answer to the inequality.

blocks.hint: The factors have opposite signs between the roots.
blocks.solution: The product is negative on \((2,6)\). At \(2\) and \(6\) it is zero.

retry.feedback: At the boundaries the product is zero. The strict inequality excludes them.

blocks.html:
Before you start

  • Adding or subtracting the same expression on both sides preserves the inequality.
  • Multiplying or dividing by a positive number preserves its direction. A negative multiplier reverses it: \(-2x<6\Rightarrow x>-3\).
  • Find quadratic roots by factorisation, completing the square, or \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\). Keep exact values when a boundary involves a square root.

An unknown expression is not a known positive number. Do not multiply or divide by \(x\) or \(x-2\) without considering its sign and whether it can be zero. The later section on fractions explains safe methods.

Write the solution clearly

MeaningInequality notationInterval notation
Between two excluded boundaries\(1<x<4\)\((1,4)\)
Include the left boundary only\(1\le x<4\)\([1,4)\)
Two outside pieces\(x<1\quad\text{or}\quad x>4\)\((-\infty,1)\cup(4,\infty)\)

Round brackets exclude a finite endpoint; square brackets include it. Infinity is never an endpoint that can be reached, so always use a round bracket next to \(\infty\) or \(-\infty\). On a number line, a hollow circle excludes a boundary and a filled circle includes it.

OR means union: keep values belonging to either set, written \(\cup\). AND means intersection: keep only values common to both sets, written \(\cap\). Thus \(x>1\) and \(x<4\) give \((1,4)\).

Be precise about what is included. In \(1\le x<4\), the input 1 is allowed, 4 is not, and every value between them is allowed. In \(x<1\quad\text{or}\quad x>4\), the two conditions are alternatives: an input does not need to satisfy both. Writing \(4<x<1\) would describe no values.

sections.title: How do I choose the correct intervals?
sections.label: Find roots, then test the sign
sections.intro: Use the roots as boundaries. Test the sign in each interval before deciding which pieces to keep.

blocks.title: Use a sign table or sketch
blocks.html:
1. Rearrange so one side is zero.
  2. Solve the related equation to find the real roots.
  3. Put the roots in increasing order and determine the sign between and beyond them.
  4. Select the intervals with the required sign. Decide separately whether zero is allowed.
  5. Apply any extra restrictions and check a value from each selected interval.

A sketch and a sign table describe the same behaviour. The sketch connects the sign to the height of the curve; the sign table explains it through the factors.
For \(f(x)=x^2+3x-10\), the negative part lies between its roots \(-5\) and \(2\). Strict inequality leaves both circles open.

figure.alt: The graph is below the x-axis between −5 and 2. Hollow circles exclude both roots.
figure.caption: Shown: f(x) < 0. The solution is (−5, 2).

blocks.title: What if equality is allowed?
blocks.html:
For the same \(f(x)\), the condition \(f(x)\ge0\) uses the two outside intervals and includes both roots.

\[(-\infty,-5]\cup[2,\infty).\]
A negative product needs opposite signs. For \((x+5)(x-2)<0\), requiring both factors to be negative would produce a positive product. A sign table keeps the two factors and their product separate.

blocks.hint: Factor \((x+2)(x-3)\). Test a value between the roots and check equality at the roots.
blocks.solution: The product is negative between \(-2\) and \(3\). Keep \((-\infty,-2]\cup[3,\infty)\).

retry.feedback: Try x = 0. The product is negative between the roots.
The comparison includes equality, so keep both roots.

sections.title: What if the roots are exact surds, repeated or absent?
sections.label: Surds, repeated roots and no roots
sections.intro: Find the exact roots if they exist. Check how the sign behaves at each one.

blocks.html: The method does not depend on neat integer factors. The boundary equation may have irrational roots, one repeated root, or no real roots. Decide which case you have before choosing a region.

blocks.solution: \((x-2)^2\le3\) gives the closed interval \([2-\sqrt3,2+\sqrt3]\).

blocks.html:
A repeated root does not change the sign

The expression \((x-2)^{2}\) is zero at 2 and positive everywhere else. Its graph touches the axis without crossing it. Therefore the four inequality signs give four different answers:

InequalityComplete solution
\((x-2)^{2}>0\)\((-\infty,2)\cup(2,\infty)\)
\((x-2)^{2}\ge0\)All real numbers: \((-\infty,\infty)\).
\((x-2)^{2}<0\)No real values: \(\emptyset\).
\((x-2)^{2}\le0\)Only \(x=2\), written \(\{2\}\).

A singleton such as \(\{2\}\) is one allowed input. The empty set \(\emptyset\) contains none. Neither means an interval extending away from 2.

Do not automatically alternate plus and minus at every root. A simple linear factor changes sign as its input passes through its root. A squared factor is positive on both sides and zero only at the root. When the same factor occurs twice, the two sign changes cancel in the product.

blocks.hint: A real square is non-negative. The only possible output is zero.
blocks.solution: \(x+1=0\) gives \(x=-1\). This single value is the whole solution.

blocks.title: Negative multiples of a square and no real roots
blocks.html:
What changes for a negative multiple of a square?

The expression \(-4(x-2)^{2}\) is zero at 2 and negative everywhere else. Dividing an inequality by −4 reverses its direction.

InequalityComplete solution
\(-4(x-2)^{2}>0\)\(\emptyset\)
\(-4(x-2)^{2}\ge0\)\(\{2\}\)
\(-4(x-2)^{2}<0\)\((-\infty,2)\cup(2,\infty)\)
\(-4(x-2)^{2}\le0\)All real numbers.

No real roots can give all values or no values

Consider \(x^{2}+2x+4=(x+1)^{2}+3\). Its least value is 3, so it is strictly positive for every real input. Consequently:

  • \(x^{2}+2x+4>0\) and \(x^{2}+2x+4\ge0\) have every real number as a solution.
  • \(x^{2}+2x+4<0\) and \(x^{2}+2x+4\le0\) have no real solutions.

For \(-x^{2}-2x-4\), every output is negative instead. The inequalities \(<0\) and \(\le0\) hold for all real inputs; \(>0\) and \(\ge0\) hold for none.

When \(D<0\), a genuine quadratic has the same sign as its leading coefficient for every real input. When \(D=0\), that sign holds away from the repeated root, where the value is zero. These cases need no invented pair of boundaries.

“Outside for greater than” is conditional. It applies to an upward-opening quadratic with two distinct real roots. Read the leading coefficient, the roots and the requested inequality together.

sections.title: How do I combine the inequality with its domain?
sections.label: Intersect conditions
sections.intro: Keep inputs that satisfy every required condition. Test each final endpoint against the original conditions.

blocks.html:
AND means intersection: keep only the values belonging to both sets, written \(A\cap B\). OR means union: keep values belonging to either set, including any overlap, written \(A\cup B\).

Two outside intervals are joined by or. A restriction such as \(x>0\) usually applies and the original inequality.

For example, \(x\le-3\) or \(x\ge5\) describes two separate intervals. Writing those conditions with “and” would ask one number to be at most \(-3\) and at least 5 simultaneously, which is impossible.

You can organise an intersection by drawing each solution on a separate number line with the same scale, then keeping only the overlap. A boundary belongs to an intersection only if every condition allows it. A boundary belongs to a union if at least one piece contains it. A closed bracket in one condition therefore cannot override an open bracket in another condition that must also hold.

Read the overlap on a number line

Intersect \(( -\infty,-1]\cup(4,\infty)\) with \((-3,6]\). Keep the portions on both number lines, giving \((-3,-1]\cup(4,6]\).

field.label: Solution set on the stated domain

blocks.hint: Find the two outside intervals, then intersect them with \((-3,6]\).
blocks.solution: The final answer is \((-3,-1]\cup[4,6]\). The domain excludes \(-3\) and includes \(6\).

retry.feedback: The original domain excludes −3. Use a round bracket at −3.

blocks.html: Check each endpoint separately. A final interval can have one open end and one closed end. The brackets follow the original conditions, not a rule that both ends must match.

sections.title: Where is one graph above another?
sections.label: Compare two outputs
sections.intro: Compare the outputs at the same input. An intersection supplies a boundary of the solution.

blocks.html: At the same input \(x\), the graph with the greater output is higher. To find when \(f(x)>g(x)\), solve \(f(x)-g(x)>0\). The intersections give boundary inputs, but the answer must describe the intervals between or beyond them.
Subtract complete expressions. If you form \(f(x)-g(x)\), bracket all of \(g(x)\) before removing the brackets. Every term in it changes sign.

blocks.solution: The line is above the parabola for \(1<x<3\). Equality holds at the two excluded boundaries.

blocks.title: Fractions and excluded values
blocks.html:
A fraction is undefined where its denominator is zero. Record those excluded values first. For a rational inequality, zeros of the numerator and denominator divide the number line into intervals on which you can check the sign.

Do not multiply by a variable expression of unknown sign. Multiplying by a negative value reverses the inequality; multiplying by a positive value does not. A sign table avoids having to guess which case applies.

sections.title: Which solutions fit the problem?
sections.label: Use the model and parameter constraints
sections.intro: Define the unknown, form the inequality and restrict the solution to values that fit the context.

blocks.html: An inequality may describe a parameter, a length, a time, or another quantity. Identify what you are finding and write down its permitted domain. The algebraic solution is a candidate set until it has been checked against the full question.

field.label: Allowed values of x in cm

blocks.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter \(20\) cm and length \(x\) cm. Its area is at least \(21\ \mathrm{cm}^2\). Give the possible values of \(x\).
blocks.hint: The second side has length \(10-x\). Solve \(x(10-x)\ge21\) with \(0<x<10\).
blocks.solution: \((x-3)(x-7)\le0\), so \(3\le x\le7\). Both boundary lengths are permitted.

blocks.title: Place both roots beyond a boundary
blocks.html:
The discriminant counts real roots, but does not locate them. For an upward-opening quadratic \(f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c\), with \(a>0\), two distinct roots are both greater than \(r\) precisely when all three conditions hold:

\[D>0,\quad h=-\frac{b}{2a}>r,\quad f(r)>0\]

\(D>0\) gives two distinct roots. \(f(r)>0\) places \(r\) outside the interval between them. The vertex condition \(h>r\) selects the outside region to the left, so both roots lie to the right of \(r\).

If equal roots are allowed, replace \(D>0\) with \(D\ge0\); keep the other two conditions strict when the roots must still be greater than \(r\).

For example, \(x^{2}-(k+2)x+2k=(x-2)(x-k)\) has roots 2 and \(k\). Both are greater than 1 when \(k>1\). If they must also be distinct, exclude \(k=2\), giving \((1,2)\cup(2,\infty)\). A real-root condition alone would miss this positional restriction.
State any defining domain or exceptional parameter values and give the complete range or set requested. For whole-number solutions, list only the integers that meet every condition.

glossary.definition: A value at which the sign or inclusion of the solution can change.
A comparison with \( < \) or \( > \), excluding equality.
Inputs common to both solution sets.
Inputs belonging to either solution set.
There are no permitted inputs.

revision.body:
From a comparison to a solution set

  1. Move everything to one side. Reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative constant.
  2. Solve the boundary equation exactly. Mark the roots in order.
  3. Test the sign in every interval. Include a root for \(\le\) or \(\ge\) if it is in the domain.
  4. Intersect the result with any domain or other condition. Check each endpoint.

Read the sign from a sketch

For \(f(x)=x^2+3x-10\), \(f(x)<0\) gives \((-5,2)\). The condition \(f(x)\ge0\) gives \((-\infty,-5]\cup[2,\infty)\).

CaseHow to decide
Two distinct rootsTest left, between and right. An upward parabola is positive outside the roots.
Repeated rootThe sign stays the same on both sides. For \((x-2)^2\le0\) the answer is \(\{2\}\).
No real rootsThe sign is the sign of the leading coefficient everywhere.

Combine and interpret

AND means intersection. OR means union. Square brackets include a finite bound. Round brackets exclude it. Always use a round bracket beside infinity.

To compare \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\), test the sign of \(f(x)-g(x)\). Record any excluded denominator values first. A context can add positive-length or integer restrictions.
revision.checks: Try a value from each interval. Keep zero values only when permitted. Give the complete solution set, with each bound included or excluded correctly.
revision.examTip:
• Show the required method and all working. Use your calculator to check.
  • Keep exact values through your working. Give non-exact answers to 3 significant figures unless the question gives another accuracy.

examples.title: A product that must be negative
examples.question: Solve \(x^{2}+3x-10<0\).
solution:
\[x^{2}+3x-10=(x+5)(x-2)\]

Find two numbers with product −10 and sum 3.

\[\begin{gathered}(x+5)(x-2)=0,\\x=-5\text{ or }x=2.\end{gathered}\]

These roots divide the number line into three intervals.

Expression\(x<-5\)\(-5<x<2\)\(x>2\)
\(x+5\)−++
\(x-2\)−−+
Product+−+

Inside each interval, neither factor passes through zero, so its sign stays the same. For instance, \(x=0\) gives \((5)(-2)=-10\), confirming the negative middle interval. The upward-opening parabola lies below the x-axis there.

\[-5<x<2\]

Select the negative product. Exclude both roots because the inequality is strict.

\[x\in(-5,2)\]

Give the complete interval, not just the two boundary values.

examples.title: A negative leading coefficient
examples.question: Solve \(-3x^{2}+9x+30\ge0\).
solution:
\[x^{2}-3x-10\le0\]

Divide both sides by −3. Reverse \(\ge\) to \(\le\).

\[(x-5)(x+2)\le0\]

Factorise the new quadratic. Its roots are −2 and 5.

\[-2\le x\le5\]

The upward-opening transformed quadratic is non-positive between its roots, including both endpoints.
You can also read the original downward-opening parabola: it is above or on the x-axis between −2 and 5. Both approaches give \([-2,5]\). As a check, \(x=0\) gives \(30\ge0\).

examples.title: Rearrange before finding the boundaries
examples.question: Solve \((x+2)^{2}\ge3x+10\).
solution:
\[x^{2}+4x+4\ge3x+10\]

Expand the squared bracket, including the middle term.

\[x^{2}+x-6\ge0\]

Subtract the whole right-hand side. Subtraction does not reverse the inequality.

\[(x+3)(x-2)\ge0\]

Factorise the difference, then find the boundaries −3 and 2.

\[x\le-3\quad\text{or}\quad x\ge2\]

The difference is non-negative outside the two roots. Equality is allowed at both.

The answer is \((-\infty,-3]\cup[2,\infty)\). Check the original comparison: at \(x=3\), the left side is 25 and the right side is 19, so this selected input works. At \(x=0\), the statement \(4\ge10\) is false, agreeing with the rejected middle interval.

The graph to inspect is the graph of the difference \(x^{2}+x-6\). Solving \((x+2)^{2}=0\) would find where the left side alone is zero, which does not answer where it equals or exceeds the right side.

examples.title: Keep surd boundaries exact
examples.question: Solve \(x^{2}-6x+2\le0\).
solution:
\[x^{2}-6x+2=0\]

Find the boundaries using the related equation.

\[x=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{36-8}}{2}=3\pm\sqrt{7}\]

The quadratic formula gives two exact real roots.

\[3-\sqrt{7}\le x\le3+\sqrt{7}\]

The quadratic opens upwards, so select the interval between the roots. Include both because zero is allowed.

The answer is \([3-\sqrt{7},3+\sqrt{7}]\). Decimal estimates can help position the roots on a sketch, but rounding changes the exact boundary. At \(x=3\), the expression is −7, confirming the selected interval.

examples.title: A restricted domain and integer answers
examples.question: Solve \(x^{2}-2x-15\ge0\) for \(-4<x\le7\). Then list the integer solutions.
solution:
\[x^{2}-2x-15=(x-5)(x+3)\]

The boundary equation has roots \(-3\) and 5.

\[x\le-3\quad\text{or}\quad x\ge5\]

The upward-opening quadratic is non-negative outside the roots. Equality is allowed, so include both roots.

\[(-4,-3]\cup[5,7]\]

Intersect with \((-4,7]\). The domain excludes \(-4\) but includes 7.

\[x=-3,\quad5,\quad6,\quad7\]

Only now select the integers from the permitted intervals. Do not round interval endpoints to obtain an integer answer.
Check a boundary: \(x=-3\) makes the quadratic zero and satisfies the domain, so it is included. Although \(x=-4\) satisfies the quadratic inequality, the stated domain excludes it.

examples.title: A double inequality
examples.question: Solve \(2\le x^{2}-2x<8\). Both comparisons must hold.
solution:
\[3\le(x-1)^{2}<9\]

Complete the square: \(x^{2}-2x=(x-1)^{2}-1\). Add 1 to all three parts.

\[x\le1-\sqrt{3}\quad\text{or}\quad x\ge1+\sqrt{3}\]

The lower bound requires the square to be at least 3. Keep both sides of the centre \(x=1\).

\[-2<x<4\]

The upper bound gives \(-3<x-1<3\). These endpoints are excluded because the inequality is strict.

\[(-2,1-\sqrt{3}]\cup[1+\sqrt{3},4)\]

Take the overlap. Include the boundaries coming from equality with 3; exclude those coming from the strict upper bound 9.

Why are there two pieces? Squaring removes the sign of \(x-1\). A sufficiently negative value and a sufficiently positive value can both produce a square of at least 3. Keeping only \(x-1\ge\sqrt{3}\) would lose the entire left-hand part of the answer. The upper bound then cuts off the distant ends of both pieces.

examples.title: A line above a parabola
examples.question: Find the values of \(x\) for which the line \(y=2x+3\) lies strictly above the curve \(y=x^{2}-3x-3\).
solution:
\[2x+3>x^{2}-3x-3\]

Translate “line above curve” into a comparison of their outputs at the same \(x\).

\[x^{2}-5x-6<0\]

Subtract the line from the curve. The difference must be negative because the curve is lower.

\[(x-6)(x+1)<0\]

Factorise the difference. Its zeros, \(-1\) and 6, are the intersection inputs.

\[-1<x<6\]

The difference is negative between its roots. Exclude both intersections because equal heights do not mean strictly above.
Quick check: at \(x=0\), the line has height 3 and the curve has height \(-3\), so the line is above. If the wording were “at least as high as”, the answer would instead be \([-1,6]\).

examples.title: A first sign check · No factor cancels
examples.question: For \(\frac{x+1}{x-4}>0\), the critical inputs are \(-1\), where the numerator is zero, and 4, where the expression is undefined.
solution:
\[x<-1:\quad\frac{\text{negative}}{\text{negative}}>0\]

Both factors are negative, so their quotient is positive. Keep this interval.

\[-1<x<4:\quad\frac{\text{positive}}{\text{negative}}<0\]

The signs differ, so this interval does not satisfy the inequality.

\[x>4:\quad\frac{\text{positive}}{\text{positive}}>0\]

Both signs are positive. Keep this interval as well.

The solution is \((-\infty,-1)\cup(4,\infty)\). The endpoint \(-1\) is excluded because zero is not strictly positive. The endpoint 4 is excluded for a different reason: the original expression is undefined there. For a non-strict inequality, a numerator zero may be allowed; a denominator zero never is.

examples.title: Cancelling leaves a hole
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x-2}\le0\).
solution:
\[x\ne2\]

The original denominator is zero at 2. This restriction stays in force throughout the solution.

\[\frac{(x-2)(x-3)}{x-2}=x-3,\quad x\ne2\]

Cancel the common factor only for inputs where it is nonzero. The simplified expression has the same value on the original domain.

\[x-3\le0\quad\Rightarrow\quad x\le3\]

Solve the remaining linear inequality, then restore the excluded input.

InputOriginal fractionAllowed?
\(x<2\)NegativeYes
\(x=2\)UndefinedNo
\(2<x<3\)NegativeYes
\(x=3\)ZeroYes
\(x>3\)PositiveNo

\[(-\infty,2)\cup(2,3]\]

The hole at 2 is excluded even though the inequality allows equality. Equality can include a zero of the expression; it cannot make an undefined expression valid.

examples.title: A parameter and an exceptional case
examples.question: Find \(p\) such that \((p-1)x^{2}+2x+1=0\) has two distinct real solutions.
solution:
\[p\ne1\]

The equation must remain quadratic. At \(p=1\), it becomes \(2x+1=0\), which has only one solution.

\[D=2^{2}-4(p-1)=8-4p\]

Use the discriminant of the equation in \(x\). The resulting inequality will be solved for \(p\).

\[8-4p>0\quad\Rightarrow\quad p<2\]

Distinct real roots require a positive discriminant. Dividing \(-4p>-8\) by \(-4\) reverses the inequality.

\[(-\infty,1)\cup(1,2)\]

Combine \(p<2\) with \(p\ne1\). Exclude 2 because it gives a repeated root.
If the question instead asked for at least one real solution, both \(p=1\) and \(p=2\) would be allowed, giving \(p\le2\). The wording determines the final set.

examples.title: An area threshold
examples.question: A rectangle has perimeter 24 cm. One side has length \(x\) cm. Find the values of \(x\) for which its area is at least \(32\text{ cm}^{2}\).
solution:
