\[\begin{gathered}\text{Other side}=12-x,\\0<x<12.\end{gathered}\]

The two adjacent side lengths add to half the perimeter. Both lengths must be positive.

\[x(12-x)\ge32\]

Area is the product of the lengths. “At least” means greater than or equal to.

\[x^{2}-12x+32\le0\]

Rearrange and multiply by \(-1\), reversing the inequality.

\[(x-4)(x-8)\le0\]

The upward-opening quadratic is non-positive between its roots, including the endpoints.

\[4\le x\le8\]

Every value in this interval also satisfies \(0<x<12\). The answer gives lengths in centimetres.
At either endpoint the area is exactly 32 cm², so both are included. An input such as \(x=6\) gives area 36 cm² and provides an interior check.

examples.title: Roots give the boundaries
examples.question: For which real \(x\) is \((x-1)(x-4)<0\)?
solution: Find where the factors are zero. The boundaries are \(1\) and \(4\).
Between them, \(x-1\) is positive and \(x-4\) is negative. Outside, the two factors have the same sign.
The product is negative between the boundaries. The inequality is strict, so the answer is \(1<x<4\), or \((1,4)\).

orig_quadratics_simultaneous.description: Solve linear and quadratic simultaneous equations by substitution. Find complete coordinate pairs and interpret intersections and tangency in 9709 Pure 1.

sections.title: What is a simultaneous solution?
sections.label: Find matching pairs
sections.intro: One ordered pair solves the system when the same two coordinates satisfy both equations.

blocks.html:
Algebra and graphs describe the same condition.

A point on a graph satisfies its equation. A point where two graphs meet satisfies both equations, so its coordinates solve the system.

figure.alt: The line y=x+2 meets the parabola y=x²−2x−2 at (−1,1) and (4,6).
figure.caption: Each intersection is one ordered pair that solves both equations.

blocks.hint: Substitute both coordinates into each original equation.
blocks.solution: For \(x=1\), the line and curve both give \(y=2\). The shared point is \((1,2)\).

blocks.html:
Another common point is \((4,6)\). The solutions are the two pairs \((-1,1)\) and \((4,6)\), not every possible combination of \(x=-1,4\) with \(y=1,6\). For example, \((-1,6)\) is not on the line.

Recognise the equations

TypeExamplesWhat to notice
Linear\(2x+y=7\), \(x=3\)The unknowns occur only to the first power, with constant coefficients.
Quadratic relation\(y=x^2+2x\), \(x^2+y^2=25\), \(xy=6\)The highest total degree in the unknowns is two. In \(xy\), the powers add to two.

The quadratic equation does not have to be written as \(y=f(x)\). It may contain \(y^2\), \(xy\), or more than one of these terms. The same substitution idea still applies.

Before you start

  • Rearrange a linear equation: \(x+2y=9\Rightarrow x=9-2y\).
  • Expand a whole bracket: \((3-y)^2=9-6y+y^2\). The middle term matters.
  • Solve a quadratic completely: use factorisation, completing the square, or \(t=\frac{-B\pm\sqrt{B^2-4AC}}{2A}\) for \(At^2+Bt+C=0\), where \(A\ne0\).

sections.title: How do I solve by substitution?
sections.label: Substitute and recover every pair
sections.intro: Use the linear equation to replace one unknown. Solve the remaining equation and find the partner of each root.

blocks.html:
Rearrange → substitute → solve → pair → check.

Use the linear equation to express one unknown in terms of the other. Replace it everywhere in the second equation, solve the resulting equation, and recover its matching coordinate for every root.

retry.feedback: This is one intersection. Solve the other factor to find the second pair.
This is one intersection. Solve the other factor to find the second pair.
The x-values are correct. Find each corresponding y-value from the line.

blocks.html:
Why is this valid? If the line says \(y=x+2\), every common point must use that value of \(y\). Putting \(x+2\) into the curve tests which points on the line also lie on the curve. Substitution reduces two conditions in two unknowns to one equation in one unknown.

Choose the easier unknown to replace

You do not have to make \(y\) the subject. Look for a coefficient of 1 or −1 in the linear equation, or a rearrangement that avoids unnecessary fractions. Keep the final coordinate order as \((x,y)\) even if you solve for \(y\) first.
Keep zero roots. From \(x(x-4)=0\), write \(x=0\) or \(x=4\). Dividing by \(x\) would discard a possible solution. Factor first, then check every candidate in the original system.

sections.title: How do I substitute in squares and products?
sections.label: Replace every occurrence
sections.intro: Write the replacement in brackets before you expand a square or multiply terms.

blocks.html:
If \(y=5-x\)The replacement isReason
\(y^2\)\((5-x)^2\)Square the whole value of \(y\).
\(xy\)\(x(5-x)\)Multiply \(x\) by the whole replacement.
\(x^2+xy+y^2\)\(x^2+x(5-x)+(5-x)^2\)Replace both occurrences of \(y\).
A square of a sum is different from a sum of squares. \((x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2\). From \(x+y=7\) you can conclude \((x+y)^2=49\), but you cannot conclude \(x^2+y^2=49\).

blocks.prompt: Substitute \(y=4-x\) into \(x^2+y^2=10\). After expanding and moving all terms to the left, what is the coefficient of \(x\)?
blocks.solution: The equation is \(2x^2-8x+6=0\), so the linear coefficient is \(-8\).

retry.feedback: Squaring \(4-x\) produces the middle term \(2(4)(-x)\).

blocks.html:
Horizontal and vertical lines

If the line gives a constant directly, substitute it directly. For \(x=2\) and \(x^2+y^2=13\), you get \(y^2=9\), so the points are \((2,3)\) and \((2,-3)\). Keep both signs. For \(x=2\) and \(y=x^2+1\), there is just one point, \((2,5)\); this vertical line is not tangent to that parabola.

These examples show why you should inspect the equation that actually remains after substitution instead of assuming that every system has two different roots in \(x\).

sections.title: How do I keep fractions and surd pairs exact?
sections.label: Give complete exact coordinate pairs
sections.intro: Keep each root with the coordinate it produces. Retain fractions and surds until the final answer.

blocks.html:
A simultaneous solution is a pair of values that satisfies both original equations. Finding the possible values of one variable is an intermediate step. Substitute each one back to find its own partner, then write the results as ordered pairs.

Keep fractions and square roots exact throughout the working. An early decimal approximation changes the value being substituted and can make a valid pair appear to fail a check. If the question requests a decimal answer, round the final coordinates to the stated accuracy.

retry.feedback: The fractional pair is correct. Remember the pair from the other factor.

blocks.html: Two x-values and two y-values do not give four solutions. Each root determines its partner through the original equation. Never mix the first x-value with whichever y-value is convenient.

sections.title: When are there two, one or no intersections?
sections.label: Count intersections and find tangents
sections.intro: Use the discriminant of the equation after substitution, provided that equation is genuinely quadratic.

blocks.html:
Suppose a valid substitution produces \(Ax^{2}+Bx+C=0\), with \(A\ne0\), and each resulting x-value determines one permitted y-value. The discriminant \(D=B^{2}-4AC\) then counts the distinct real intersection points.

DiscriminantEliminated equationSimultaneous solutions
\(D>0\)Two distinct real rootsTwo distinct coordinate pairs
\(D=0\)One repeated real rootOne coordinate pair
\(D<0\)No real rootsNo real coordinate pairs

For a line and a non-degenerate circle or parabola in this quadratic situation, the repeated-root case represents tangency. Count the repeated root once: writing the same point twice does not create two intersections.

How the intercept changes the solution pairs

For the curve \(y=x^2-4x+8\) and the line \(y=2x+k\), substitution gives \((x-3)^2=k+1\). The lines for \(k=3\), \(k=-1\) and \(k=-3\) show the two-point, tangent and no-intersection cases.
Use the discriminant after substitution. The discriminant of \(x^{2}-4x+8=0\) concerns the curve's intersections with the x-axis. It does not count intersections with an arbitrary line.

blocks.prompt: The line \(y=4x-3\) is tangent to \(y=x^2+1\). Find the contact point.
blocks.solution: The repeated root is \(x=2\). Substitute in the line to get \(y=5\), so the point is \((2,5)\).

blocks.html:
Important exception: one intersection need not mean tangency

Check that the eliminated equation is genuinely quadratic before using its discriminant. A vertical line can give a single point directly: \(x=2\) and \(y=x^{2}\) give \((2,4)\), although the line is not tangent.

Parameters can also remove the squared term. Consider \(xy=4\) and \(y=mx+1\).

\[mx^{2}+x-4=0\]

Substitution gives a quadratic only when \(m\ne0\).

\[\begin{gathered}m=0:\quad x-4=0\\\Rightarrow(x,y)=(4,1)\end{gathered}\]

Handle the exceptional value separately. The horizontal line has one crossing with the hyperbola; this is not a tangent.

\[m\ne0:\quad D=1+16m\]

Now the discriminant test is valid. The repeated-root case occurs at \(m=-\frac1{16}\).

\[\begin{gathered}m=-\frac1{16}\Rightarrow(x-8)^{2}=0\\\Rightarrow(x,y)=(8,\frac12)\end{gathered}\]

This is the tangent case. Thus exactly one simultaneous solution occurs at \(m=0\) or \(m=-\frac1{16}\), but only the latter gives tangency.

blocks.title: A known point or separation between intersections
blocks.html:
The point \((1,6)\) lies on both \(y=x^{2}+ax+4\) and \(y=bx+2\). Find the parameters and the other intersection.

\[\begin{gathered}6=1+a+4\Rightarrow a=1\\6=b+2\Rightarrow b=4\end{gathered}\]

Substitute the known coordinates into each original equation. A point on both graphs must satisfy both conditions.

\[\begin{gathered}x^{2}+x+4=4x+2\\\Rightarrow(x-1)(x-2)=0\end{gathered}\]

Now use the determined equations. The known x-coordinate, 1, is one root.

\[x=2\Rightarrow y=10\Rightarrow(2,10)\]

This is the other intersection; do not report the given point as the new one.

A condition on the distance between the x-coordinates can determine a parameter too. In the earlier family \(y=x^{2}-4x+8\), \(y=2x+k\), the roots are \(3\pm\sqrt{k+1}\). Their separation is \(2\sqrt{k+1}\). If that separation is 6, then \(k+1=9\), so \(k=8\); the points are \((0,8)\) and \((6,20)\).

For a general genuine quadratic, the separation of its two real roots is \(\frac{\sqrt{D}}{|A|}\). This is a horizontal separation; it is not the straight-line distance between the two intersection points.

sections.title: Which pairs are valid in the original problem?
sections.label: Model, restrict and check
sections.intro: Set up the original equations and domain before solving. Test each resulting pair against both conditions.

blocks.html:
In a word problem, define each variable and its units before forming equations. Identify the linear relationship and the quadratic relationship separately. Write down physical restrictions such as positive lengths or non-negative times; these are part of the problem.

Restrictions can also be mathematical. A point may be required to lie in a stated quadrant or interval. A denominator in an original equation must remain nonzero, even if a later simplification hides it. Apply these conditions to each complete pair, not just to one coordinate.

blocks.prompt: A rectangle has area \(45\ \mathrm{cm}^2\). Its length is \(4\) cm more than its width. Give the pair (width, length).
blocks.solution: \((w-5)(w+9)=0\), so \(w=5\) is the permitted width and the length is \(9\). The pair is \((5,9)\).

retry.feedback: The algebraic pair is negative. The model requires both lengths to be positive.

blocks.html: If a question asks for an intersection point, give both coordinates. If it asks for a tangent parameter and the point of contact, provide both results. If there are no real solutions, state that clearly instead of leaving the answer blank.

blocks.title: Both intersection x-coordinates positive
blocks.html:
Suppose valid substitution gives a genuine quadratic \(Ax^{2}+Bx+C=0\), with \(A\ne0\). If its real roots are \(r\) and \(s\), expanding \(A(x-r)(x-s)\) and comparing coefficients gives

\[r+s=-\frac BA,\qquad rs=\frac CA.\]

There are two distinct positive roots precisely when all three conditions hold:

\[D>0,\qquad-\frac BA>0,\qquad\frac CA>0.\]

The discriminant gives distinct real roots. A positive product makes them nonzero and of the same sign; the positive sum selects the positive sign. This criterion does not assume that \(A\) is positive.

For example, consider \(y=x+c\) and \(x^{2}+y^{2}=8\). Their x-coordinates satisfy \(2x^{2}+2cx+c^{2}-8=0\).

\[D=64-4c^{2}>0\Rightarrow-4<c<4\]

Require two distinct intersections.

\[r+s=-c>0,\qquad rs=\frac{c^{2}-8}{2}>0\]

Require a positive sum and product as well.

\[-4<c<-2\sqrt2\]

Intersect the three conditions. At the left boundary the points coincide; at the right boundary one x-coordinate is zero.

These conditions concern the x-coordinates only. Recover the matching y-coordinates when requested and check any additional restrictions on them.

blocks.title: Before you move on
blocks.html:
1. Set up: identify the two equations and any original restrictions.
  2. Substitute: isolate a convenient variable, replace every occurrence and keep brackets.
  3. Solve: simplify to one equation and find all real candidates, keeping exact values.
  4. Pair: find the matching value of the other variable for each candidate.
  5. Check and report: test both original equations and the domain; give full coordinate pairs or the requested quantities with units.

glossary.definition: An ordered pair satisfying both equations.
Replace a variable with an expression equal to it.
The x-coordinate followed by its matching y-coordinate.
A point that lies on both graphs.
A shared point where the line and curve have the same gradient.

revision.body:
Rearrange, substitute, solve, pair, check

  1. Make one variable the subject of the linear equation. Choose the simpler rearrangement.
  2. Replace every occurrence in the other equation. Square the entire bracket when needed.
  3. Solve the resulting equation exactly, keeping every candidate.
  4. Find the other coordinate for each candidate. Write ordered pairs \((x,y)\).
  5. Check both equations and any domain or physical restrictions.

One intersection is one matching pair

For \(y=x+2\) and \(y=x^2-2x-2\), equating the outputs gives \((x+1)(x-4)=0\). The pairs are \((-1,1)\) and \((4,6)\).

How many pairs?

If valid substitution gives a genuine quadratic and each root gives one permitted partner, use its discriminant. Two distinct roots give two pairs, a repeated root gives one pair and a negative discriminant gives none.

For a non-vertical line and parabola, the repeated-root case shows tangency. A single solution can also come from a linear equation or a vertical line. Check the equation after substitution.
revision.checks:
• Replace every occurrence, including products and squared terms.
  • Keep signs paired correctly in surd coordinates. Use fractions and surds until the final answer.
  • Apply restrictions to each full pair. For tangency give the coordinates of the contact point when asked.
revision.examTip:
• Show the required method and all working. Use your calculator to check.
  • Keep exact values through your working. Give non-exact answers to 3 significant figures unless the question gives another accuracy.

examples.title: A line and a parabola
examples.question: Solve \(y=x+2\) and \(y=x^2-2x-2\).
solution:
\[x+2=x^2-2x-2\]

The linear equation already gives \(y\). At a common point, the two expressions for \(y\) must agree.

\[x^2-3x-4=0\]

Bring every term to one side. Keep the equation equal to zero before factorising.

\[(x-4)(x+1)=0\]

Use two numbers with product −4 and sum −3.

\[x=4\quad\text{or}\quad x=-1\]

Either factor can be zero. These are the first coordinates, so the solution is not finished yet.

RootReturn to \(y=x+2\)Matching pair
\(x=-1\)\(y=-1+2=1\)\((-1,1)\)
\(x=4\)\(y=4+2=6\)\((4,6)\)
Check each pair in both original equations. For \((4,6)\), the line gives \(6=4+2\) and the curve gives \(6=16-8-2\). The check for \((-1,1)\) was shown in the first section. Both pairs work.
Complete answer: \((x,y)=(-1,1)\quad\text{or}\quad(4,6)\).

examples.title: Solve for y first
examples.question: Solve \(x+2y=9\) and \(xy=10\).
solution:
\[x=9-2y\]

This rearrangement has no denominator. Making \(y\) the subject would also be valid, but would introduce a fraction.

\[\begin{gathered}(9-2y)y=10\\\Rightarrow 2y^2-9y+10=0\end{gathered}\]

Replace the whole factor \(x\) in the product. The remaining equation involves only \(y\).

\[(2y-5)(y-2)=0\]

The roots are \(y=\frac52\) and \(y=2\).

\[\begin{gathered}y=\frac52\Rightarrow x=4\\y=2\Rightarrow x=5\end{gathered}\]

Use the same linear relation for both roots.
The solutions are \((4,\frac52)\) and \((5,2)\). Both products are 10, and both values of \(x+2y\) are 9.

examples.title: A line and a circle
examples.question: Solve \(x+y=7\) and \(x^2+y^2=25\).
solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y=7-x\\x^2+(7-x)^2=25\end{gathered}\]

Use the linear equation, then substitute into the circle equation. You do not need to rearrange the circle into square roots.

\[\begin{gathered}2x^2-14x+24=0\\\Rightarrow(x-3)(x-4)=0\end{gathered}\]

Divide every term by 2 before factorising.

\[\begin{gathered}x=3\Rightarrow y=4\\x=4\Rightarrow y=3\end{gathered}\]

The matching points are \((3,4)\) and \((4,3)\). These are distinct points even though the same two numbers occur.
Both pairs have sum 7 and square-sum 25. The line therefore crosses the circle at two points. A sketch helps interpret the answer; the algebra gives its exact coordinates.

examples.title: A mixed quadratic relation
examples.question: Solve \(x+y=5\) and \(x^2+xy+y^2=19\).
solution:
\[x^2+x(5-x)+(5-x)^2=19\]

Substitute \(y=5-x\) into both \(xy\) and \(y^2\).

\[\begin{gathered}x^2+(5x-x^2)\\{}+(25-10x+x^2)=19\end{gathered}\]

Expand before collecting terms. The first two quadratic terms cancel, but another remains.

\[\begin{gathered}x^2-5x+6=0\\\Rightarrow(x-2)(x-3)=0\end{gathered}\]

The two roots are 2 and 3.

\[(x,y)=(2,3)\quad\text{or}\quad(3,2)\]

Return to \(y=5-x\). Each pair has sum 5 and satisfies \(x^2+xy+y^2=4+6+9=19\).

A useful second way to see the structure

Since \((x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2\), the two given equations imply \(25=19+xy\), so \(xy=6\). Substituting \(y=5-x\) gives the same quadratic. Different sound algebraic routes must produce the same complete pairs.

examples.title: A fractional coordinate
examples.question: Solve \(y=2x+1\) and \(y=2x^{2}+7x-2\).
solution:
\[2x+1=2x^{2}+7x-2\]

At an intersection, both expressions give the same value of \(y\) for the same input \(x\).

\[2x^{2}+5x-3=0\]

Collect every term on one side before factorising.

\[\begin{gathered}(2x-1)(x+3)=0\\\Rightarrow x=\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad x=-3\end{gathered}\]

Set each factor equal to zero. From \(2x-1=0\), divide by 2 to obtain the fractional root.

\[\begin{gathered}x=\frac12\Rightarrow y=2\\x=-3\Rightarrow y=-5\end{gathered}\]

Use the linear equation separately for each root.

\[(x,y)=(\frac12,2)\quad\text{or}\quad(-3,-5)\]

Each coordinate pair is a complete solution. The order of the two solutions does not matter; the order of the coordinates within a pair does.

Check both equations: for \((\frac12,2)\), the line gives \(2(\frac12)+1=2\), while the curve gives \(2(\frac12)^2+7(\frac12)-2=2\). For \((-3,-5)\), the two expressions give \(-6+1=-5\) and \(18-21-2=-5\).

examples.title: The signs in a surd pair are linked
examples.question: Solve \(x+y=3\) and \(x^{2}+y^{2}=13\), giving exact answers.
solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y=3-x\\x^{2}+(3-x)^{2}=13\end{gathered}\]

Replace the whole of \(y\) by \(3-x\), keeping brackets around the expression being squared.

\[\begin{gathered}2x^{2}-6x-4=0\\\Rightarrow x^{2}-3x-2=0\end{gathered}\]

Expand the square, collect terms, then divide the equation by 2.

\[x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{17}}2\]

The discriminant is 17, so the quadratic formula gives two irrational roots.

\[y=3-\frac{3\pm\sqrt{17}}2=\frac{3\mp\sqrt{17}}2\]

Subtracting the chosen \(x\) reverses its square-root sign. A plus sign in \(x\) must go with a minus sign in \(y\).

\[(\frac{3+\sqrt{17}}2,\frac{3-\sqrt{17}}2)\]

This is the pair obtained from the larger value of \(x\).

\[(\frac{3-\sqrt{17}}2,\frac{3+\sqrt{17}}2)\]

This is the pair obtained from the smaller value of \(x\).

The symbols \(\pm\) and \(\mp\) describe linked choices: take the top sign in both expressions, or the bottom sign in both. Writing out the two pairs makes this explicit. Choosing both plus signs would give \(x+y=3+\sqrt{17}\), so that combination is not a solution.
An exact check is possible without decimals. For either correct pair, \(x+y=3\) and \(xy=\frac{9-17}{4}=-2\). Therefore \(x^{2}+y^{2}=(x+y)^{2}-2xy=9+4=13\).

examples.title: Find a parameter for tangency
examples.question: The curve is \(y=x^{2}-4x+8\). The line is \(y=2x+k\). Find the values of \(k\) giving two, one or no real intersections. Find the point of contact in the one-intersection case.
solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x^{2}-4x+8=2x+k\\\Rightarrow x^{2}-6x+8-k=0\end{gathered}\]

First combine the two equations. It is the discriminant of this new quadratic that counts their intersections.

\[\begin{gathered}D=(-6)^{2}-4(1)(8-k)\\{}=4(k+1)\end{gathered}\]

Keep brackets around the parameter expression when subtracting \(4AC\).

\[k>-1:\quad\text{two intersections}\]

A positive discriminant gives two distinct pairs.

\[k=-1:\quad\text{one intersection}\]

A zero discriminant gives the tangent position of the line.

\[k<-1:\quad\text{no real intersections}\]

A negative discriminant means no point satisfies both real equations.

\[\begin{gathered}k=-1\Rightarrow (x-3)^{2}=0\\\Rightarrow x=3,\quad y=5\end{gathered}\]

Substitute the parameter back, find the repeated root, then use the line \(y=2x-1\). The point of contact is \((3,5)\).

The curve also gives \(3^{2}-4(3)+8=5\), confirming the contact point. Another way to see the threshold is \((x-3)^{2}=k+1\): a positive right side gives two x-values, zero gives one, and a negative right side gives none.

examples.title: Two tangents through one fixed point
examples.question: Find the tangent lines to \(y=x^{2}+1\) that pass through \((0,-3)\). A non-vertical line through this point has equation \(y=mx-3\).
solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x^{2}+1=mx-3\\\Rightarrow x^{2}-mx+4=0\end{gathered}\]

Form the intersection equation before imposing the tangent condition.

\[\begin{gathered}D=m^{2}-16=0\\\Rightarrow m=4\quad\text{or}\quad m=-4\end{gathered}\]

Both square roots must be considered. There are two tangent slopes, not one.

\[y=4x-3:\quad(x,y)=(2,5)\]

For the positive slope, the intersection equation is \((x-2)^{2}=0\).

\[y=-4x-3:\quad(x,y)=(-2,5)\]

For the negative slope, it is \((x+2)^{2}=0\). Both lines pass through the required fixed point.
The vertical line through \((0,-3)\) has equation \(x=0\). It crosses the parabola at \((0,1)\), where the tangent is horizontal.

examples.title: Dimensions of a rectangle
examples.question: A rectangle has area 60 cm². Its length is 4 cm greater than its width. Find its dimensions.
solution:
\[\begin{gathered}l=w+4,\quad wl=60\\w>0,\quad l>0\end{gathered}\]

Let \(w\) be the width and \(l\) the length, both in centimetres. Difference gives the linear equation; area gives the product equation.

\[\begin{gathered}w(w+4)=60\\\Rightarrow w^{2}+4w-60=0\end{gathered}\]

Replace the length by its expression in terms of the width.

\[\begin{gathered}(w+10)(w-6)=0\\\Rightarrow w=-10\quad\text{or}\quad w=6\end{gathered}\]

Find every algebraic candidate before applying the physical restriction.

\[(w,l)=(-10,-6)\quad\text{or}\quad(6,10)\]

Recover the corresponding length for each width. The negative pair satisfies the equations but cannot describe lengths.

\[\begin{gathered}\text{Width}=6\text{ cm}\\\text{Length}=10\text{ cm}\end{gathered}\]

Keep the positive dimensions and include units in the final answer.

Check the original statements: \(10-6=4\) and \(6\times10=60\). Rejecting the negative pair does not mean the quadratic was solved incorrectly. The model has a smaller permitted domain than the algebraic equations alone.

examples.question: Is \((-1,1)\) on both \(y=x+2\) and \(y=x^2-2x-2\)?
solution: Use \(x=-1\) in the line: \(-1+2=1\). This agrees with \(y=1\).
Use \(x=-1\) in the curve: \(1+2-2=1\). The same ordered pair satisfies both equations.
